a-wagyu-bbq.text: Eric Zhou opened A+ Wagyu BBQ in 2025 as a follow-up to his nearby Chinese hot pot restaurant Palace Tang, taking a Courtyard Shops storefront that had sat empty since the French bistro Mikette left in 2020. The cook-at-your-table Korean barbecue trades on the quality of its meat, including M9 Australian and A5 Japanese Wagyu beef.
a-wagyu-bbq.descriptor: Cook-at-your-table Korean BBQ on Plymouth Rd in the Courtyard Shops

afternoon-delight.descriptor: Breakfast and lunch cafe on E. Liberty St. downtown

ahmos.descriptor: Mediterranean counter for gyros, shawarma and Mediterranean fries

alley-bar.descriptor: Small downtown bar at 112 W. Liberty St., a block off Main

allmendinger-park.text: G. Frank Allmendinger gave the city the first 3.25 acres in 1917, naming the park for his grandfather John George Allmendinger, who settled in Washtenaw County in 1832. In 2012 artist Mary Thiefels built "Nourishing Healthy Seeds," a community mosaic on the shelter pillars, with help from neighbors and Slauson Middle School students.
allmendinger-park.descriptor: Eight-acre park on Pauline Blvd with ballfields, courts and a shaded playground

ama-bistro.text: A local, family-owned and operated spot on South State within walking distance of the University of Michigan campus, aMa serves breakfast, lunch and dinner. The dinner menu is where the family's authentic Albanian dishes turn up, sitting alongside Italian pasta and burgers, while lunch runs to sandwiches, wraps, salads and soups.
ama-bistro.descriptor: Family-run cafe at 215 S. State; breakfast, lunch and Albanian dinner dishes

amadeus.text: The Ann Arbor Observer calls Amadeus "Ann Arbor's refined Polish-Hungarian restaurant." It was founded by Krystyna Aniolczyk, whose son Bart grew up in its kitchen before going on to open his own barbecue place, Jake's BBQ Shack, in Dexter.
amadeus.descriptor: Polish-Hungarian restaurant at 122 E. Washington St.

amers-delicatessen.text: Amer's has fed University of Michigan students from its State Street counter across from the Diag for more than 30 years, with a menu that runs from Mediterranean falafel and tabbouleh to New York bagels with lox and capers and a customizable acai bowl made with 100% acai. Owner Amer often works the counter himself, and staff are known for remembering regulars by name and order.
amers-delicatessen.descriptor: Mediterranean deli and cafe on S. State St. across from the Diag

ann-arbor-golf-and-outing-club.text: The club was formally organized on September 26, 1899 by Scottish University of Michigan professors, and after it bought its own 40 acres in 1903 the members plowed and seeded the cornfield and pastureland, then let sheep keep the grass down. In 1925 Fielding Yost eyed the grounds as a site for Michigan Stadium; the members said no, so the Big House went up across the street.
ann-arbor-golf-and-outing-club.descriptor: Private nine-hole club on 32 acres at 400 E Stadium Blvd, founded 1899

writtenFor.name: Ann Arbor Golf and Outing Club

ann-arbor-hands-on-museum.text: The museum opened in 1982 inside Ann Arbor's 1882 central fire station, which the fire department had vacated four years earlier. It now packs more than 250 interactive exhibits on physics, geology, math, music and technology into the old firehouse, and draws over 200,000 visitors a year.
ann-arbor-hands-on-museum.descriptor: Interactive science museum in the 1882 firehouse at Ann & Fifth

anthonys-gourmet-pizza.text: Anthony's has been baking Chicago-style deep dish in stone hearth ovens in Ann Arbor since 1988, alongside New York-style and Sicilian pies. The N. Maple Road shop is one of two in town; the other is on Packard Street.
anthonys-gourmet-pizza.descriptor: Chicago deep-dish and stone-hearth pizza on N. Maple Rd since 1988

argo-nature-area.text: Argo Dam was built by Detroit Edison in 1920 to generate power, decommissioned in 1959, and bought by the city in 1963; the flat water behind it, Argo Pond, is where Michigan and local high school crews row. In 2012 the city opened the Argo Cascades alongside it — nine small drops falling about 12 feet over 1,200 feet, so paddlers can ride around the dam instead of portaging.
argo-nature-area.descriptor: 22-acre Huron River park with trails, a canoe livery and the Argo Cascades

argus-farm-stop-packard-cafe.text: Argus is a "farm stop" — a year-round market where the farmers own the produce, set their own prices and keep 70% of the sale — a model Kathy Sample and Bill Brinkerhoff brought to Ann Arbor in 2014. The second shop opened in August 2017 at 1200 Packard in the old Clague's Market building, and expanded in 2022 into a larger space a block up at 1226 Packard. Argus says it has paid over $26 million to local farms.
argus-farm-stop-packard-cafe.descriptor: Second Argus farm stop on Packard Rd, open since 2017

argus-museum.text: Argus began as the International Radio Corporation in 1931, making plastic-cased Kadette radios, and pivoted to cameras with the $12.50 Argus A in 1936. Its C3 rangefinder — the boxy "brick" — was made from 1939 until 1966, passing two million units. The museum occupies the second floor of the Argus building at 525 W. William St.
argus-museum.descriptor: Museum of Argus cameras on the 2nd floor of the old Argus plant, 525 W. William St.

ashleys-ann-arbor.text: Ashley's has poured beer a few steps from campus at 338 S. State St. since 1983, billing itself as Michigan's Premium Multi-Tap with a global list spanning Belgian beers, Bohemian, South German, Pacific Northwest and Michigan styles. It also runs a serious whiskey program, with a Scotch collection and curated flights.
ashleys-ann-arbor.descriptor: Multi-tap craft beer pub at 338 S. State St. since 1983

asian-legend.text: Kevin Lo, born in Taiwan and in the U.S. since 1983, opened Asian Legend on E. William in 2007, later knocking through into the neighboring storefront that had been David's Books to double his seating. Alongside the Americanized Chinese menu he runs a Taiwanese section with stinky tofu and mustard greens, spicy pork intestine, and pig feet with basil.
asian-legend.descriptor: Taiwanese and Szechuan cooking on E. William, open since 2007

aventura.text: Restaurateur Sava Farah bought this 1872 building and found an antique table the previous owner had left behind. The room's old-world feel — brick arches and original stonework — suggested tapas, so she and her team went to Spain to research, and came back with Aventura. That table, "La Mesa," still anchors the dining room.
aventura.descriptor: Spanish tapas and paella in an 1872 building at 216 E. Washington St.

baba-dari.text: Baba Dari says it carries on the story of Ali Baba's, the Middle Eastern restaurant it grew out of, at 601 Packard just off campus. The counter is best known for chicken shawarma and lamb kebab bowls, plus falafel, hummus and baba ganoush.
baba-dari.descriptor: Halal Mediterranean grill on Packard — shawarma bowls, kebabs, falafel

backroom-pizza.text: Students call it Dollar Pizza — cheese slices a buck, topped slices a quarter more. It sits half a block south of South University, serves the same pizza as the Brown Jug, and stays open late, which makes it the standard last stop of a night out.
backroom-pizza.descriptor: Late-night dollar-slice window on Church St, half a block off South University

bader-park.text: The park is named for Edith M. Bader, an Ann Arbor assistant superintendent from 1921 to 1942, and occupies the grounds of the Bader Elementary School that closed in 1985. After Fellowship Bible Church bought the property in 1987, disputes over public access led the city to condemn the park space in 1995 to keep it as public parkland.
bader-park.descriptor: 1.5-acre park with playground and half-court off Provincial Drive

bandemer-park.text: Bandemer was a railroad stockyard, and parts of it were used as a dumping ground during M-14 construction in the 1950s before the city reclaimed it; the Johnson-Greene riverfront parcel was acquired in the early 1980s with help from the Bandemer Trust Fund, an estate bequest. Its 38 acres hold a nine-hole disc golf course built in 2007, a dirt bike jump course, and rowing docks used by U-M, Huron High and the Ann Arbor Rowing Club.
bandemer-park.descriptor: 38-acre Huron River park with rowing docks and a disc golf course

bandemer-park-disc-golf.text: The nine-hole course was built in 2007 inside Bandemer Park, 38 acres on the Huron River just west of Argo Pond that the city began assembling in 1974 and reclaimed from a former railroad stockyard, dumping ground and highway staging area. Dirt footpaths wind through the holes with river views, and the park doubles as a Border-to-Border Trail head with a dirt-jump bike course and the Ann Arbor Rowing Club boathouse at its south end.
bandemer-park-disc-golf.descriptor: Nine-hole disc golf course in Bandemer Park, built in 2007

bao-space.text: Bao Space bills itself as the first specialized restaurant bringing hand-made Asian bao buns to Ann Arbor, steamed fresh daily at 205 N. Main. Past the buns the menu runs to dumplings, dim sum, soups, salads and bubble tea, and the kitchen leans on Berkshire pork, wild-caught shrimp and organic Michigan-grown mushrooms.
bao-space.descriptor: Hand-made steamed bao bun specialist at 205 N. Main downtown

barton-nature-area.text: Detroit Edison built Barton Dam here in 1912 — the tallest on the Huron River at the time — and the pond behind it still supplies most of Ann Arbor's drinking water. The city bought the property from Edison in the 1960s. A plant inventory of the old-field oxbow recorded 324 species, and a trail network with two bridges built in 1991 now carries the Border-to-Border Trail.
barton-nature-area.descriptor: 98-acre Huron River park at the Barton oxbow, with dam and Border-to-Border Trail

bearclaw-coffee-co.text: On November 19, 1931 a Cadillac pulled into the two-level gas station on Washtenaw Ave; men with dark goggles and hats pulled over their eyes left a five-gallon jug painted with Michigan–Minnesota football scores going back to 1903, then drove off. It was said to be the stolen Little Brown Jug, though the Ann Arbor Daily News called it an imitation and Minnesota's equipment manager scoffed at it. Bearclaw Coffee is there today.
bearclaw-coffee-co.descriptor: Drive-thru coffee on Washtenaw Ave, on an old gas station site

beckley-park.text: The park honors Guy Beckley, the abolitionist minister who published Ann Arbor's antislavery newspaper the Signal of Liberty in the 1840s; the nearby Guy Beckley House was a stop on the Underground Railroad. Locals mostly know the three-acre park for its long sloping hill, which the city lists as open for unsupervised sledding.
beckley-park.descriptor: North-side park with a sledding hill, petanque court and playground on Argo Drive

belize-park.text: Dedicated on June 16, 1975, the park is named for Belize City, one of Ann Arbor's sister cities. Words carved into its wooden retaining wall read "In memory of Essie Logan who resided here," honoring residents killed in a 1965 house fire on the site. The rain garden, added in 1992, was rebuilt in 2016 and won a Rain Garden Leadership Award in Public Stewardship.
belize-park.descriptor: Half-acre neighborhood park with a sledding hill and an award-winning rain garden

bennys-family-dining.text: Benny's has been serving breakfast on S. Industrial since 2000, and its most famous regular was Michael Phelps — a server told Current magazine she used to bring the swimmer his morning food while he trained in Ann Arbor with coach Bob Bowman ahead of the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
bennys-family-dining.descriptor: All-day breakfast and family diner on S. Industrial Hwy since 2000

berts-cafe.text: Bert's Cafe opened in February 2008 in the Shapiro Undergraduate Library. It's named for Bertram Askwith (LSA '31), who donated it and also funded the Askwith Media Library, on the building's second floor.
berts-cafe.descriptor: Coffee and pastry counter in U-M's Shapiro (UGLi) library

bills-beer-garden.descriptor: Seasonal outdoor beer garden downtown, open March through October

bird-hills-nature-area.text: At 146 acres, Bird Hills is Ann Arbor's largest natural area — unpaved trails through hills and ravines above the Huron River, on land the city bought in 1968 after it had been logged, grazed and terraced as a fruit orchard. The out-of-place conifers, including Scots pine and Douglas fir, were planted by Henry Graves and his nephew in the early 1900s to sell a subdivision that never got built.
bird-hills-nature-area.descriptor: 146-acre wooded nature area off Newport Rd, the city's largest

black-diesel-coffee.text: Nick Ferris opened Black Diesel in 2015 in the corner storefront at Packard and E. Stadium that had housed Caribou Coffee and Peet's, both of which left when their corporate owners pulled out of the region. It began as a multiroaster cafe pouring other roasters' beans, and Ferris also founded BD Barista School, a certified Specialty Coffee Association training campus.
black-diesel-coffee.descriptor: Multiroaster coffee bar at the corner of Packard and E. Stadium

black-pond-woods-nature-area.text: Black Pond is a vernal pond whose basin was formed by a slow-melting remnant of glacial ice; tannins and humic acids from leaf litter stain the water dark brown and give it its name, and because it fills entirely from rainfall and usually dries out by summer, no fish live in it. The city bought the remaining 34 acres in June 1991 for $1,175,000 — the Michigan DNR covered 75 percent — after residents fought off a housing development, and a floating boardwalk went in in 1997.
black-pond-woods-nature-area.descriptor: 34-acre woods and glacial vernal pond between Traver Rd and Pontiac Trail

blazin-coops-nashville-hot-chicken.descriptor: Halal Nashville hot chicken spot at 1800 Plymouth Rd

blm-mead-cider.text: Founders Lauren and Matt started Bløm after Matt — a brewer and co-owner of Chicago's Begyle Brewing — developed a gluten intolerance and turned to mead and cider. Their session meads are light, dry and carbonated, fermented like a craft cider rather than thick and sweet, and the ingredients are Michigan-sourced.
blm-mead-cider.descriptor: Downtown taproom at 100 S Fourth Ave pouring session meads and ciders

blue-apple.text: The Blue Apple opened in 2006 as a $2.2 million dining "emporium" inside the Bursley Hall dorm on U-M's North Campus, selling pizza, paninis, smoothies and snacks on Dining Dollars or Blue Bucks. Students rarely use the full name — to them it's "the Blapple."
blue-apple.descriptor: Cafe in Bursley Hall serving pizza, paninis and snacks on U-M's North Campus

blue-leprechaun.text: The Blue Leprechaun opened on South University in 2008, taking over the former Touchdown Cafe at 1220 S. University, and spent seventeen years as a campus-bar fixture — gameday menus, long happy hours — before closing on December 13, 2025.
blue-leprechaun.descriptor: South U Irish pub and student bar, 2008-2025

blue-nile-ethiopian.descriptor: Ethiopian restaurant on E. Washington St. downtown

bluffs-nature-area.text: The city describes Bluffs as a roughly 40-acre tract sitting on a glacially formed ridge, an important link in the corridor of natural areas surrounding the Huron River. Footpath trails wind throughout with a lot of ups and downs, some quite steep, and the park has long been a favorite place for bicycles. The city also notes that the largest collection of butternut trees in Ann Arbor can be found here, along with hickories and uncommon understory plants.
bluffs-nature-area.descriptor: 40-acre wooded nature area off N. Main with steep, winding footpaths

bodega-bros.text: Esam Almulaiki, a Hamtramck native whose family runs five delis in Queens, Brooklyn and the Bronx, opened Bodega Bros in 2023 in the old Silvio's Organic Pizza space at 715 N. University. Handing out free smoothies, juices and desserts outside — routine bodega manners in New York — he told the Ann Arbor Observer that "everybody was looking at me like I'm crazy." An early favorite was the $6.50 bacon, egg and cheese roll.
bodega-bros.descriptor: New York–style bodega deli at 715 N. University, open late

broadway-cafe.text: The menu is famously short — a handful of Korean dishes plus a cheesesteak hoagie — and the signature item splits the difference: bulgogi beef piled on a soft bun with melted cheese and sauteed onions. An Observer cheap-eats review found the crowd split about half and half between the Korean plates and the sandwich.
broadway-cafe.descriptor: Tiny Korean-and-cheesesteak-hoagie counter at 1139 Broadway St

broadway-park.text: The city assembled this riverfront land mostly by condemnation between 1902 and 1915 and designated it Riverside Park in 1907, but locals called it "Hobo Park" from about 1934 until it was officially renamed Broadway Park in 1973. Today the five acres hold a 1.37-acre fenced dog park with separate areas for larger and smaller dogs, plus Turbine, a 2015 sculpture made from repurposed canoes.
broadway-park.descriptor: Five-acre Huron River park off Broadway with a fenced dog park

broadway-park-west.text: Broadway Park West opened in September 2025 on the site of a Michigan Consolidated Gas coal gasification plant — the Huron River itself was rerouted in 1915 to make room for the plant. Cleanup in 2023–24 hauled out 13,000 tons of polluted soil, part of the largest brownfield redevelopment in Washtenaw County history. Phase one added trails, river access and a bridge to the county's Border-to-Border Trail.
broadway-park-west.descriptor: Seven-acre riverfront park on Broadway St., on a former gas-plant brownfield

bromley-park.text: Developer Brooks Barron dedicated the land to the city in 1963 as North Campus Heights Park; it was renamed Bromley in 1986 after a new subdivision, and the Kiwanis Club finished a new play area the following year. A neighbor has kept up the rose garden for decades, and a small wooded grove holds the Bromley Book Box, a little free library.
bromley-park.descriptor: Playground, rose garden and little free library off Briarcliff Street

btb-burrito.text: Two students back from studying abroad opened it in 2003 as Big Ten Burrito. The Big Ten Conference objected to the name, so the shop ran a renaming contest that drew over 1,000 entries and came out the other side as BTB. This State Street spot between Hill and Packard is the flagship.
btb-burrito.descriptor: Burrito counter at 810 S. State, between Hill and Packard

burger-one.text: Burger One is an all-halal burger joint in a strip mall on Plymouth Road north of campus, serving burgers, chicken tenders and milkshakes. It bills itself as a halal burger franchise that grew "from a small local business to a multi-location restaurant," though Ann Arbor is the only location currently listed — and it's closed Sundays.
burger-one.descriptor: Halal burger counter on Plymouth Rd. — burgers, tenders, shakes

burns-park.text: Burns Park sits on the site of a half-mile horse track that the Ann Arbor Driving Club ran until 1920; the city had bought the land in 1910 and named it for George Burns, a botany professor who helped build the city's park system. The 15 acres now hold ball fields, three tennis courts and two pickleball courts, a pétanque court and a playground, with Burns Park Elementary along the west edge and the Ann Arbor Senior Center in the southeast corner.
burns-park.descriptor: 15-acre neighborhood park off Baldwin Ave. with ballfields and tennis

burr-oak-park.text: The land was set aside as public parkland under the escrow agreement for the 1989 Liberty Glen subdivision, and the homeowners association still runs a park workday here every May. In August 2021 and again in September 2022, the city's Adopt-a-Park program brought in a herd of goats from Twin Willow Ranch to graze down invasive shrubs and poison ivy.
burr-oak-park.descriptor: 3.3-acre far-west-side park split by Burr Oak Drive, with native-plant gardens

bursley-dining-hall.text: Bursley is the largest dormitory at the University of Michigan, housing approximately 1,300 students on North Campus, so its dining hall feeds a small town. A $4.5 million renovation in summer 2016 rebuilt the food service area into five distinct stations, each dedicated to a particular type of cuisine, and the building also holds the Blue Market convenience store.
bursley-dining-hall.descriptor: North Campus dining hall inside Bursley, U-M's largest residence hall

cafe-verde.text: Cafe Verde has operated out of the People's Food Co-op on North Fourth Avenue since 2001, remodeled in 2004, pouring fair-trade coffee alongside baked goods and items from the co-op's hot and salad bar. The co-op itself has been on the block since 1971.
cafe-verde.descriptor: Fair-trade coffee bar inside the People's Food Co-op on N. Fourth Ave

cafe-zola.descriptor: Downtown cafe on W. Washington St., with a second bistro on Washtenaw

cantina.text: It started in 2004 as BTB — Big Ten Burrito — on State Street, modeled on the burritos its founders knew from growing up in Santa Barbara, and later moved upstairs above Good Time Charley's on South U. Owners Adam Lowenstein and Justin Herrick then dropped the BTB name and relaunched it as Cantina, a taqueria and bar, while keeping Taco Tuesday.
cantina.descriptor: Student taqueria and bar upstairs on South University

cardamom.text: Binod Dhakal came from Nepal in 1995 and managed Shalimar on Main from the late 1990s before opening Cardamom at the end of April 2013, in the old Famous Hamburgers space in the Plymouth Rd Courtyard Shops — the opening-weekend line ran out the door. Nepali momos and a multi-dish thali lunch special are the draw; a 2015 expansion added the bar and its cardamom-syrup Old Fashioned.
cardamom.descriptor: Indian-Nepali kitchen on Plymouth Rd, known for hand-wrapped momos

casa-dominicks.descriptor: Longtime local restaurant at 812 Monroe St. in Ann Arbor

caseys-tavern.text: Casey's was carved out of the old Washtenaw Lumber Co. office on Depot Street by developer Bill Martin nearly forty years ago, and has been a classic townie hangout for burgers and pub grub ever since. A much larger second location later opened on the east side, off Plymouth Road in the former Carson's American Bistro space.
caseys-tavern.descriptor: Townie tavern in a former lumberyard office on Depot St, known for burgers

cedar-bend-nature-area.text: One of Ann Arbor's oldest parks: the city bought the land in small parcels in the late 1890s, transferred it to the new Park Commission in May 1905, and hired landscape architect O.C. Simonds that December, whose principle was that "no landscape gardener can plant as well as nature has planted." Steep unpaved trails climb the slope and ridge past the hairpin turn, a remnant of an old road that traced the river's sharp bend.
cedar-bend-nature-area.descriptor: 19-acre wooded slope above a sharp bend of the Huron River, off Cedar Bend Dr

chans-garden.descriptor: Chinese restaurant in Ann Arbor, formerly Chan's Garden, now branded Chan Garden

chapala-mexican-restaurant.text: Cesar Ochoa opened Chapala in the summer of 2020 in the N. Main space vacated by the three-year-old Agave Tequila Bar. He set out to serve "what Mexicans eat when they go out" at prices that wouldn't feel stuffy; the signature empapelado marino brings shrimp, scallops and tilapia out inside half a pineapple.
chapala-mexican-restaurant.descriptor: Mexican restaurant and bar at 211 N. Main St., open since 2020

chelas-restaurant-taqueria.text: Adrian Iraola spent about 25 years as an inspector and architectural engineer for the City of Ann Arbor before he and his wife Lori opened the first Chela's — named for his mother — in the small strip center at Maple and Liberty in 2012. The recipes run in the family: his great-grandmother catered weddings in Mexico City, and his father sold tacos and tortas from stands at his parking lots.
chelas-restaurant-taqueria.descriptor: Mexican street-food taqueria at Maple and Liberty since 2012

chicago-reds.descriptor: Chicago-style Vienna Beef hot dog counter inside Amer's Deli on S. State

churchill-downs-park.text: The city acquired this 1.18-acre park around 1970 and put in a new playground in 2018. A $3.2 million stormwater management basin meant to cut neighborhood flooding was completed in November 2022, along with a trail connecting the park south to Eisenhower Park.
churchill-downs-park.descriptor: Playground and half-court park on Steeplechase Dr near Scio Church Rd

cloverdale-park.text: The city acquired Cloverdale in 1960 when the surrounding neighborhood's development was approved. It connects to the wooded strip known as the Missing Link — green space set aside in the 1950s for road access that was never used for that purpose. The playground went in in 1999, and trees were planted the following year after a neighborhood controversy over trees that had been cut down.
cloverdale-park.descriptor: Hilly 1.75-acre neighborhood park on Cloverdale Rd, west of Pontiac Trail

comet-coffee.text: Comet hides at 16 Nickels Arcade — the glass-roofed shopping passage off State Street, finished in 1918 and described as perhaps the only remaining free-standing commercial arcade building in Michigan. Its coffee has a following among local baristas: the owner of Espy Cafe worked at Comet before opening his own place.
comet-coffee.descriptor: Small independent coffee bar tucked inside Nickels Arcade

community-food-forest-at-leslie-park.text: A partnership between Ann Arbor Parks and Recreation and volunteers since 2020, the food forest layers fruit trees, berry bushes, herb, tea, medicinal and pollinator gardens the way a woodland stacks canopy and understory. It sits within 38-acre Leslie Park, land the city acquired from Eugene and Emily Leslie in 1963 — a gift that also seeded the golf course and the Leslie Science and Nature Center.
community-food-forest-at-leslie-park.descriptor: Volunteer-tended fruit, berry and herb food forest inside Leslie Park

writtenFor.name: Community Food Forest at Leslie Park

connor-oneils.text: Conor O'Neill's was designed in Ireland: the front room copies a rural "shop pub," with timber floors and shelves for merchandise, while the back is built around a cottage room meant for storytelling and music. Irish bric-a-brac throughout nods to Irish music, literature, sport and history, and a trad Irish session runs every Sunday.
connor-oneils.descriptor: Irish pub at 318 S. Main St., designed in Ireland

cosa-sabrosa.text: Chef-owner Jeff Gardner launched Cosa Sabrosa — "tasty thing" — as a food truck in 2016, tracked down by followers on Facebook. In January 2021 he moved the operation indoors at the Zal Gaz Grotto, a Masonic lodge on W. Stadium Blvd, serving eight fillings across tacos, burritos and nachos, from beef, pork, fish and chorizo to sweet potato and cauliflower.
cosa-sabrosa.descriptor: Mexican taqueria inside the Zal Gaz Grotto club on W. Stadium Blvd

cottage-inn-pizza.text: Cottage Inn started in 1948 at 512 E. William St. near campus — a coffee business that added pizza and is credited with being the first place in Ann Arbor to serve it. Franchising began in Ypsilanti in 1986, and the chain now runs more than 50 locations across Michigan and Ohio.
cottage-inn-pizza.descriptor: Branch of the Ann Arbor pizza chain founded in 1948

cottage-inn-pizza-lakewood.text: Cottage Inn began in 1948 at 512 E. William St. as a coffee business that added pies, making it the first place in Ann Arbor to serve pizza; the Michos family bought the original building in 1961. Carryout and delivery arrived in 1978 and franchising in 1986, and the company says it passed 75 stores across Michigan, Ohio and Indiana by its 75th anniversary in 2023. This is the Packard Street shop near campus.
cottage-inn-pizza-lakewood.descriptor: Carryout pizza on Packard near campus; Cottage Inn started in Ann Arbor in 1948

cottage-inn-pizza-packard-street.text: Cottage Inn opened in 1948 on E. William St. as Ann Arbor's first pizzeria, added carryout and delivery in 1978, and opened its first franchise in Ypsilanti in 1986; the company says it passed 75 stores across Michigan, Ohio and Indiana by 2023. This is the northeast-side store on Plymouth Road.
cottage-inn-pizza-packard-street.descriptor: Northeast-side pizza carryout on Plymouth Rd; Ann Arbor chain founded 1948

crary-park.text: Douglas Crary, a University of Michigan geography professor who also served on the Ann Arbor City Council and Planning Commission, acquired this corner lot after a fire destroyed the house on it and kept it as open greenspace for more than 45 years. After he died in 2006, his daughters donated the land to Ann Arbor, and the city formally accepted it as parkland on Dec. 28, 2007.
crary-park.descriptor: 1.3-acre corner park at Washtenaw Avenue and Cambridge Road

creal-park.text: A 1.5-acre pocket park tucked between Creal Crescent and Argyle Crescent northwest of downtown, with a full basketball court, a lighted asphalt path linking the two streets, an open field, and play structures with swings and a merry-go-round.
creal-park.descriptor: Neighborhood park on Creal Crescent with a basketball court and merry-go-round

crisler-center.text: Opened December 6, 1967 and named for longtime athletic director Fritz Crisler, the arena is nicknamed "the House That Cazzie Built": star Cazzie Russell drew basketball crowds too big for Yost Field House, which is what forced the university to build it. It seats about 12,707 and got a $52 million renovation completed in 2012.
crisler-center.descriptor: Michigan basketball arena since 1967, "the House That Cazzie Built"

cupsnchai.text: CupsnChai is a Michigan-born South Asian café built around karak chai, served alongside street food, flatbreads and desserts. Its franchise pitch is "born in Michigan, brewed for North America" — the downtown Ann Arbor shop is one of two Michigan locations, with a sibling in Canton, and the company is now selling franchises.
cupsnchai.descriptor: South Asian chai and street-food café on S. Fourth Ave. downtown

curious-coffee.text: Mike Bawden, a British-born coffee hobbyist who moved here in 2023 when his wife, an art historian, took a named U-M professorship, turned home roasting into Curious Coffee: lightly roasted single-origin beans he sources himself, water he remineralizes to his own recipe, and a no-laptops policy. It started as a residency inside Bløm Mead + Cider at 100 S. Fourth Ave., then opened its own shop at 217 N. Main in early May 2026.
curious-coffee.descriptor: Small-batch light-roast specialty coffee roaster and cafe, downtown

curry-on.text: Owners Rutul Patel and Swetang Patel (no relation, despite the shared surname) first opened as Curry Up, then renamed the place Curry On in March 2014 after Palo Alto's Curry Up Now, which was expanding nationally, objected to the name. The Plymouth Rd. counter does kati rolls, samosa chaat and biryani on a heavily vegetarian menu, plus jalebi and gulab jamun for dessert.
curry-on.descriptor: Indian street-food counter on Plymouth Rd — kati rolls and samosa chaat

deborah-gimbel-memorial-overlook.text: A named lookout in Nichols Arboretum, the University of Michigan's 128-acre landscape park, established in 1907 and best known for its Main Valley long view and its heirloom peony garden. The view from the overlook carries toward North Campus and the Ann & Robert H. Lurie Carillon — a favorite vantage point in fall color.
deborah-gimbel-memorial-overlook.descriptor: Named memorial overlook in Nichols Arboretum, with a view toward North Campus

depot-plaza.text: Acquired by the city in 1967 as a right-of-way deed, this flower-garden sliver at Main and Depot is billed by Parks and Recreation as Ann Arbor's smallest park property, and it welcomes drivers coming off the M-14 exit onto Main Street. A pedestrian tunnel off Depot Street connects north to Bandemer and Argo parks on the Border-to-Border trail.
depot-plaza.descriptor: Ann Arbor's smallest park: a flower garden at Main and Depot streets

detroit-observatory.text: U-M president Henry Philip Tappan pitched it in an 1852 speech and Detroit businessmen paid for it — which is why an Ann Arbor building is named for Detroit. Its 12 5/8-inch Fitz refractor was the third-largest refracting telescope in the world when it was installed in 1857, and director James Craig Watson used the place to discover 22 asteroids between 1863 and 1877.
detroit-observatory.descriptor: 1854 University of Michigan observatory, now a campus museum

detroit-street-filling-station.text: The Lunch Room's Phillis Engelbert and Joel Panozzo went from vegan pop-up dinners in 2010 to a cart at Mark's Carts to a Kerrytown storefront, then opened this all-vegan, full-service restaurant in August 2017. It sits in the historic Staebler Family Oil Company filling station on Detroit St., a building that had housed Argiero's Family Italian Restaurant for four decades.
detroit-street-filling-station.descriptor: Vegan restaurant in a restored Staebler oil-company filling station, Kerrytown

devonshire-park.text: Just over an acre, Devonshire Park is really a shortcut: a paved, snow-plowed path cutting between Devonshire Road and Geddes Avenue that gives the surrounding neighborhood a walking connection to Gallup Park and, beyond it, the Furstenberg Nature Area.
devonshire-park.descriptor: 1.16-acre connector park with a path from Devonshire Rd to Geddes Ave

dicken-elementary-plant-garden.text: A former Dicken parent and a group of volunteers cleared a 20-by-20-foot square of school lawn in spring 2010 and started planting. It has grown into a volunteer-run outdoor classroom — vegetables, milkweed planted by Girl Scouts to draw monarchs, a shed, and a woodland and butterfly area certified as a wildlife habitat — with families adopting plots to keep it tended over the summer.
dicken-elementary-plant-garden.descriptor: Volunteer-run school garden at Dicken Elementary, started in 2010

dicken-park.text: Barely half an acre of mowed grass on Maple Road at Tudor Drive, it is named for Carrie L. Dicken, who taught in Ann Arbor Public Schools for four decades. She helped bring about Perry School in 1902, founded a night school in 1913 to help newly arrived immigrants, and was principal of Bach School until she retired in 1934.
dicken-park.descriptor: Half-acre mowed-grass neighborhood park on Maple Road at Tudor Drive

dicken-woods-nature-area.text: Neighbors formed the Friends of Dicken Woods to keep this 10-acre parcel from being built on, and the city bought it in 2004. Traces of its farming past survive — an old foundation, apple trees from the orchard, even strawberry plants — and a boardwalk crosses a seasonal wetland at the headwaters of the Allen and Mallets creek watersheds. A trail extension runs onto Dicken Elementary property.
dicken-woods-nature-area.descriptor: 10-acre woods and vernal ponds off S. Maple Rd, saved from development in 2004

dimos-deli-donuts.text: It opened in 1973 as an Amy Joy Donuts franchise and became Donut's Time after that chain folded. In 1991 the Dimo family — Karim and Mary — added breakfast, deli sandwiches and Mediterranean dishes alongside the donuts.
dimos-deli-donuts.descriptor: Donuts, breakfast and deli sandwiches on W. Stadium Blvd since 1973

don-juan-mexican-bar-grill.text: The West Stadium Boulevard Don Juan is one of two Ann Arbor restaurants in the Los Amigos Don Juan group, which has nine locations across Michigan and Ohio and describes itself as a family dream built on recipes passed down through generations. The kitchen sticks to traditional plates — tacos al carbon, the Molcajete Maya, mojarra frita and coctel de camaron — alongside the margaritas, a local favorite.
don-juan-mexican-bar-grill.descriptor: Mexican bar and grill at 2135 W. Stadium Blvd with margaritas and molcajetes

douglas-park.text: The land was donated in 1928 to honor Henry W. Douglas, a member of the city's first Board of Parks Commission, created in 1905. His father Silas Douglas taught chemistry at U-M and founded the Ann Arbor Gas Company in 1858, which Henry later ran as superintendent. Today it's a shaded 2.5-acre lawn used for frisbee, touch football and studying.
douglas-park.descriptor: 2.5-acre open lawn between Washtenaw, Baldwin and Cambridge

dr-harold-j-lockett-park.text: Renamed in December 2021 from Winchell Park by a unanimous city council vote and dedicated in June 2022, it honours Dr. Harold J. Lockett — a child psychiatrist and U-M Medical Center assistant professor who in 1969 became the school board's first Black president, under the motto "Schools are for all the children."
dr-harold-j-lockett-park.descriptor: Nearly 4.5-acre neighborhood park with ball diamond at Winchell and St. Francis

earthen-jar.text: Ann Arbor's by-weight Indian buffet: everything is vegetarian, much of it vegan, and it's priced by the pound ($10.99) rather than by the plate — a Fifth Ave. fixture since 1997. Dishes like channa masala, mattar paneer and shahi korma sabzi rotate through the steam table, with vegan, gluten-free, kosher and halal options flagged.
earthen-jar.descriptor: Pay-by-the-pound vegetarian Indian buffet on S. Fifth Ave. since 1997

east-quad-dining-hall.text: East Quad dates to 1940 and reopened in fall 2013 after a $116 million renovation whose dining hall seats 430 with station-style service — grill, pizza, deli and vegan stations. The building also houses U-M's Residential College with its 15 classrooms and studios, and the renovation removed the basement's old Halfway Inn.
east-quad-dining-hall.descriptor: U-M dining hall inside 1940s East Quad, home of the Residential College

eat-thai.descriptor: Thai kitchen on S. Main St. downtown

eberwhite-woods.text: The University of Michigan gave this patch of woods to Ann Arbor Public Schools in 1946 on the condition that it never be developed or sold. Stewardship is still mostly informal — neighbors pull invasive plants, organize trail wood-chipping days, and put up signs each spring to protect the great horned owl fledglings. Three small ponds inside are good for turtle-spotting.
eberwhite-woods.descriptor: Neighborhood woods and trails at the edge of Eberwhite Elementary

echelon-kitchen-bar.text: Echelon opened February 6, 2025 at 200 S. Main, at Main and Washington, in a century-old building that began as a Kresge five-and-dime and was most recently BD's Mongolian Grill. The kitchen is built around Michigan fruit woods, mostly cherry — roughly 250 cubic feet burned a month — and in 2026 the team added Hunã, a 4,000-square-foot tiki bar in the basement with its own W. Washington entrance.
echelon-kitchen-bar.descriptor: Wood-fired farm-to-table dining at Main and Washington, open since 2025

eda-u-gerstacker-grove.descriptor: Four-acre green at the center of U-M's North Campus, by the Lurie Tower

edible-garden.text: Friends of Greenview maintains this demonstration orchard with Pioneer High School and other volunteers as a "living classroom" of sustainable, regionally adapted food plants — on land once part of the Wuerth homestead orchard, farmed until the early 1900s. It mixes natives like paw paw, elderberry, chokeberry and wild strawberry with apricots, pear, plum, nectarine, cherry, hazelnut and hardy apple cultivars.
edible-garden.descriptor: Public fruit-and-nut orchard in the Greenview & Pioneer Woods Nature Area

eisenhower-park.text: The trails here were dug by the neighbors. Volunteer workdays ran from November 2021 through a final push on November 13, 2022 — joined by student groups from the University of Michigan — cutting an unpaved path system through the greenway. The trail now links Churchill Downs Park to the north and Dundee Drive to the south, with a connection out to Scio Church Road.
eisenhower-park.descriptor: Ten-acre greenway along I-94, just south of Scio Church Road

el-harissa-market-cafe.text: Susan Thomas, a retired teacher, and Khaled Houamed, a Tunisian-born pharmacologist and biotech CEO, opened El Harissa in 2013 after a long licensing delay — the market needed state agriculture approval and the food service a county health sign-off, and the kitchen isn't even connected to the storefront. It is named for harissa, the Tunisian chili paste, and pairs a deli case of mujadara, hummus and dips with shelves of North African groceries.
el-harissa-market-cafe.descriptor: Tunisian café, deli and market in Maple-Miller Plaza on N. Maple

el-limon.text: El Limón mixes Mexican and Mediterranean cooking at 2709 Plymouth Rd, and books local musicians across a range of genres on Monday and Thursday nights.
el-limon.descriptor: Mexican–Mediterranean kitchen on Plymouth Rd with live local music

eula-d-marcks-garden.text: A tucked-away courtyard garden at the Michigan League, set with a patio of tables and chairs beneath one large tree — a quiet study spot most students walk past without noticing. It is named for Eula dePriest Marcks, University of Michigan class of 1933, honored there along with her husband.
eula-d-marcks-garden.descriptor: Courtyard garden and patio at the Michigan League on N. University

evergreen.descriptor: Chinese restaurant at 2771 Plymouth Rd. on Ann Arbor's northeast side

evergreen-downtown.text: Greg Guo had run Evergreen on Plymouth Rd. for three decades before opening this second location at 208 W. Liberty, in the brick building behind Bill's Beer Garden that Chow Asian Street Food had occupied. The shorter menu here is pitched as modern Chinese — more seasonal and playful — with wide-noodle beef, cumin lamb and dry pot, a wok-cooked take on hot pot.
evergreen-downtown.descriptor: Modern Chinese restaurant at 208 W. Liberty, downtown offshoot of Evergreen

felch-park.text: The park is named for Alpheus Felch, Michigan's governor in 1846–47 and later a U.S. senator, who returned to Ann Arbor in his later years and died there in 1896. When the Power Center for the Performing Arts was built on the park's edge, the volume facing the park was clad in mirrored glass specifically to reflect the surrounding trees and make the green space appear larger.
felch-park.descriptor: Green space on U-M's central campus beside the Power Center on Fletcher St

fireside-cafe.descriptor: Coffee-and-sandwich café inside Pierpont Commons on U-M's North Campus

first-bite.text: First Bite opened at 108 S. Main in the space left empty when the vegetarian Back2Roots Bistro closed suddenly in late 2016, serving wraps, grain bowls, salads and smoothies built around a chickpea-beet burger and a Thai peanut wrap. As of a 2017 Ann Arbor Observer review, it billed itself as the only place in southeast Michigan where you could get kava, the South Pacific drink made from ground root.
first-bite.descriptor: Health-food counter on S. Main with wraps, bowls, smoothies and kava

fleetwood-diner.text: The Fleetwood opened in 1949 as the Dag-Wood Diner, a prefab steel lunch counter built from a Toledo diner kit, and was renamed the Fleetwood in 1971. The tiny round-the-clock counter is famous for its Hippie Hash and for feeding students, townies, artists and late-night philosophers at any hour.
fleetwood-diner.descriptor: Downtown 24-hour diner in a 1949 prefab steel car, home of the Hippie Hash

forsythe-park.text: The city bought this abandoned gas station lot in 1974 with a HUD grant for in-city parks and called it Packard/Arch Park; in 1980 it was renamed for Franklin C. Forsythe, founder and first president of the Ann Arbor Jaycees. Its I-beam sculpture, "Reduce, Reuse and Recycle," has a water fountain built into it, and the third-acre lot is a convenient cut-through for students headed to campus.
forsythe-park.descriptor: Third-acre pocket park at Packard and Arch, on a former gas station lot

franks-restaurant.text: Frank's is named for the brother-in-law who was the original partner, but the man at the griddle was Pete Poulos, who spent more than forty years flipping burgers there and cooked for the U-M football team. After a neck injury he retired and sold the diner to Tony Zervogiannis in October 2013, who kept the place almost exactly as it was.
franks-restaurant.descriptor: Small breakfast-and-lunch diner on Maynard St next to Tower Plaza

frasers-pub.descriptor: Packard Rd sports bar with a deep tap list and weekly trivia

frisinger-park.text: The Frisinger Land Co. gave this 3.6-acre corner to the city on June 15, 1936, and the softball backstop went up in 1964. It's a short walk from Michigan Stadium, with the playground and picnic tables tucked at the shaded south end, away from the traffic noise.
frisinger-park.descriptor: Neighborhood ballfield and playground at E Stadium Blvd and Woodbury Dr

frita-batidos.text: Chef-owner Eve Aronoff trained at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris but built this place around childhood summers spent with her grandmother in Miami. A frita is a chorizo burger buried under shoestring fries on a soft egg bun; a batido is a tropical milkshake of fresh fruit, crushed ice and sweetened milk. The restaurant says Michigan Daily readers have voted it the city's best burger every year since 2014.
frita-batidos.descriptor: Cuban-inspired street food downtown — chorizo fritas and tropical batidos

fritz-park.text: The land was given to the city in 1936 by Elsa Fritz DeFries, Jessie Fritz and John E. Fritz in memory of their uncle Michael J. Fritz, who served on the park commission for more than 20 years. Before that it was Ann Arbor Schutzenbund Park, a historic meeting place for German-Americans; the city annexed it in 1948. Eighty-one native plant species have been recorded here.
fritz-park.descriptor: Wooded 5-acre park on Pauline Blvd between Seventh St and Stadium Blvd

fuller-park.text: Ann Arbor's first municipal golf course ran here from the 1930s into the 1960s, nicknamed the "Rock Pile." After the University of Michigan ended its land lease in 1967 the city built the outdoor pool, and soccer fields followed by 1974. A pedestrian bridge crosses the Huron to Island Park, tying the park into the Border-to-Border trail network.
fuller-park.descriptor: 60-acre riverside park on Fuller Rd with a 50-meter outdoor pool and ball fields

furstenberg-nature-area.text: The land belonged to Albert and Elizabeth Furstenberg until 1971, when Ann Arbor bought it for $90,000 with a HUD Open Space grant; after 1990s restoration work the park had its grand opening in 1996. Its 38 acres hold wetlands, woods, prairie and oak savanna, cared for with controlled burns since 1996, and a quarter-mile of wetland boardwalk connects to Gallup Park.
furstenberg-nature-area.descriptor: 38-acre Huron River nature area with wetlands, prairie and a boardwalk

garden-homes-park.text: An 11-acre neighborhood park tucked between N. Maple Road and M-14, wooded with open lawn and more than 3,000 feet of paved path. The city developed it in 1974, and a new play structure went in in 2007 after Ann Arbor asked the surrounding neighborhood what it wanted. A rain garden along Miller Avenue, south of the main park, is part of it too.
garden-homes-park.descriptor: 11-acre wooded neighborhood park off N. Maple in northwest Ann Arbor

george-washington-park.text: This sliver of park exists for one thing: The Rock, a 23-ton boulder that parks superintendent Eli Gallup pulled from a city gravel pit and installed in 1932 for George Washington's 200th birthday. Visiting Michigan State students painted it in their colors in the mid-1950s, Michigan students painted back, and it has been repainted ever since — the buildup was about five inches thick by 2010.
george-washington-park.descriptor: Traffic-triangle park at Washtenaw and Hill, home of The Rock

get-away-n-play-cafe.descriptor: Hospital cafeteria with a Subway, floor 2 of Mott Children's Hospital

ginger-deli.text: Ginger Deli was opened in summer 2014 by Te Phan, a former automotive designer and classical pianist who describes the food as "like a watercolor painting, it's very bold but sensitive and delicate." The Vietnamese counter is known for banh mi on bread baked daily and house-made ingredients.
ginger-deli.descriptor: Vietnamese deli known for banh mi and house-baked bread

good-time-charleys.text: Open since 1979 at the corner of South University and Church, Charley's has been a fixture for Michigan students and faculty for four decades. It's known for hand-rolled Styx and Twists stuffed breadsticks, Long Island fishbowls and an outdoor patio.
good-time-charleys.descriptor: Campus bar at S. University and Church since 1979; fishbowls and Styx

grand-grounds.text: Grand Grounds opened on Aug. 7, 2024 in the shared lobby of C.S. Mott Children's Hospital and Von Voigtlander Women's Hospital at Michigan Medicine. The counter serves Zingerman's Bakehouse baked goods, coffee and specialty drinks Monday through Friday from 6:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., plus Boar's Head deli sandwiches, snacks and desserts.
grand-grounds.descriptor: Coffee bar in the Mott Children's Hospital lobby, open since 2024

graydon-park.text: Ann Arbor bought this land from the Michigan State Highway Commission for one dollar in 1966, and for decades it was Rose White Park — named simply for the Rose Avenue and White Street corner it sits on. In 2020 it was renamed Graydon Park in honor of Graydon Krapohl, a park neighbor and former city council member.
graydon-park.descriptor: Small playground park on Rose Ave near E. Stadium Blvd

greenview-nature-area.text: Greenview and Pioneer Woods Nature Area has an unusual arrangement: the land is owned by Ann Arbor Public Schools and managed jointly by the City of Ann Arbor and Friends of Greenview, a neighborhood group that has been at it for more than twenty years. Its volunteers cleared invasive buckthorn and planted demonstration pollinator gardens; the site records more than 50 butterfly species.
greenview-nature-area.descriptor: Meadow, pond and oak woods off S. Seventh St., tended by a neighbors' group

grizzly-peak-brewing-company.text: When a 2022 remodel quietly dropped the cheese curds from Grizzly Peak's post-renovation menu, an online petition launched under the name "Kim Curdashian" set out to bring them back. The brewpub promised their return if the petition hit 500 signatures by February 12; the goal was met early, and the curds came back on Valentine's Day, with signers getting a free order.
grizzly-peak-brewing-company.descriptor: Downtown brewpub at 120 W. Washington with house beer and cheese curds

haifa-falafel.text: Ali Usman was 22 when he opened the first Haifa Falafel in 2008, naming it for the Israeli port city he had left at 18. He had wanted the Courtyard Shops near North Campus but was turned down because another Middle Eastern restaurant already held the spot — seventeen years later he opened his second location in exactly that storefront. He's known for stuffing falafel inside a pocket pita instead of wrapping it.
haifa-falafel.descriptor: Made-to-order falafel and shawarma at Courtyard Shops on Plymouth Rd

hannah-park.text: A one-acre ravine tucked between houses off Mark Hannah Place, deeded to the city in 1969 by the developer of the surrounding neighborhood. Neighbors' invasive-plant removal has let native jewelweed and false Solomon's seal flourish, groundwater seeps support iris, and Cooper's hawks nest in the tall trees.
hannah-park.descriptor: One-acre wooded ravine nature area at 206 Mark Hannah Place

hanover-square.text: Ann Arbor's oldest park: created sometime between 1824 and 1836 and formally dedicated in 1859. It was literally square until 1925, when a portion was deeded to the Board of Education for the adjacent W.S. Perry school, leaving the triangle you see today; the play equipment came out in 1968. Ronald Bauer's "Arbor Sapientiae" sculpture was installed here in 1984.
hanover-square.descriptor: Half-acre triangular green at Packard and Division, the city's oldest park

happy-wok.descriptor: Chinese takeout counter at 1916 W. Stadium Blvd on Ann Arbor's west side

hazel-coffee-co.text: Hazel is a specialty coffee and matcha cafe that married owners Hailey and Bryan opened at 2111 Packard St. in fall 2025 after building a following on TikTok. The menu runs on house-made syrups - banana bread, salted maple, sugar cookie - plus pastries and breakfast burritos made with Iggy's Eggies, served daily 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.
hazel-coffee-co.descriptor: Coffee and matcha cafe at 2111 Packard St., open since fall 2025

hearsay-brewery.text: hear.say is a brewery with an improv theater attached — crisp lagers, hop-forward IPAs, fruited sours and bold stouts on one side, improv and stand-up shows most Thursday through Sunday on the other. It also runs an improv school, hear.say academy, and hosts the multi-day Yes, Ann Improv Fest.
hearsay-brewery.descriptor: Brewery and improv theater on W. Liberty St, styled hear.say

heathdale-collection.text: Heathdale is one of the named collections inside Nichols Arboretum, the 128-acre "Arb" that opened to the public in 1907 after the Chicago firm of O.C. Simonds drew up plans in 1906. It is planted with ericaceous and Appalachian species — Catawba and rosebay rhododendrons, azaleas and mountain laurel — and some of its specimens trace to plant-collecting expeditions of the 1920s.
heathdale-collection.descriptor: Rhododendron and Appalachian plant valley inside Nichols Arboretum

heidelberg-restaurant.text: The Heidelberg has served German food on N. Main since 1961, and it stacks three rooms in one building: German dining at street level, the darts-and-games Rathskeller in the basement, and the Club Above upstairs for dancing and entertainment.
heidelberg-restaurant.descriptor: German restaurant on N. Main since 1961, three floors deep

hello-faz-pizza.descriptor: Halal pizza, subs and cheesy bread carryout at 2259 W. Liberty

hibachi-san.descriptor: Japanese-style grill and rice-bowl counter inside Pierpont Commons, North Campus

hilltop-nature-area.text: Until 2006 this was Camp Hilltop, a Girl Scout camp on land donated to the Scouts in 1947; after its 1948-49 lodge burned that April, Ann Arbor bought the 7.7-acre parcel for $2.24 million with Greenbelt funds and formally named it Hilltop in 2009. Camp remnants like a marker and flagpole still stand along trails with spectacular views of the Huron River valley and spring wildflowers.
hilltop-nature-area.descriptor: Hilltop woods above the Huron River valley, on a former Girl Scout camp

hola-seoul.text: Hola Seoul opened at 715 N. University in September 2019 with Korean barbecue tacos as its hook — pre-marinated meat with soy-vinaigrette lettuce, carrots, cabbage and house pickled onions. Owner Sung Hee Kim emigrated from South Korea and helped run the Manna Asian market on Broadway before moving into restaurants; her sushi-and-noodle spot Mama Satto sits next door in Roumanis Square.
hola-seoul.descriptor: Korean-Mexican fusion on N. University; Korean tacos and fried chicken

holidays-restaurant.text: Owner Rob TerBush keeps a fireplace and a decorated tree going year-round, re-trimming the tree for Mother's Day, St. Patrick's Day, Valentine's Day and the rest — hence the motto "where every day's a celebration." He also plants vegetable and herb gardens outside that the kitchen cooks from, and a help-yourself bookshelf he started for bored kids is now stocked by customers.
holidays-restaurant.descriptor: Family comfort-food diner on W. Stadium Blvd since about 1997

hollway-field.text: Hollway Field is Ann Arbor Pioneer High School's football stadium, named for Lou Hollway, a longtime athletic teacher at the school. It is also the home ground of AFC Ann Arbor — "The Mighty Oak" — the USL League Two club founded in 2014 that returned to this original home in 2023 after stints at Skyline High, Concordia and Saline.
hollway-field.descriptor: Pioneer High football stadium, home ground of AFC Ann Arbor soccer

hollywood-park.text: The city got these three acres in 1961 from the subdivision's developer, and in 1964 a crew clearing undergrowth drew protests from neighbors and students. Parks director S.S. Sproull defended the work — "Mother Nature can display considerable beauty without having poison ivy entwined in her hair" — then met residents in 1965 and compromised. It still has one of the city's richest spring wildflower displays.
hollywood-park.descriptor: Three-acre woodland park by Abbot Elementary off Sequoia Parkway

holocaust-memorial.text: The seated, grieving bronze figure is the work of sculptor Leonard Baskin, erected in 1994. It stands in Raoul Wallenberg Plaza next to U-M's Rackham Building, named for the 1935 University of Michigan graduate who saved tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews in 1944.
holocaust-memorial.descriptor: Leonard Baskin bronze in Wallenberg Plaza beside U-M's Rackham Building

homes-brewery.text: HOMES is the schoolroom mnemonic for the Great Lakes — Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior — and the water theme runs down to the extensive underground stormwater retention system at the property. Tommy Kennedy opened it on Jackson Ave in April 2017 with head brewer Nick Panchame, and the house style has stayed hop-forward ales and sours.
homes-brewery.descriptor: West-side brewpub at 2321 Jackson Ave, hoppy and sour beers

hopcat.text: HopCat started in Grand Rapids in 2008 and grew into a Michigan beer-bar chain built on enormous tap lists. Its signature fries spent years as "Crack Fries" until the company renamed them "Cosmik Fries" in December 2018 — after the Frank Zappa song "Cosmik Debris" — to avoid making light of crack cocaine addiction.
hopcat.descriptor: Michigan craft-beer bar at 311 Maynard St., known for Cosmik Fries

hot-pot-chen.text: Despite the name, there is no tabletop hot pot here: it is a Chinese-American takeout counter at 2255 W. Stadium Blvd. whose closest thing to the namesake is a run of "Earthen Pot" clay-pot dishes like ginger basil chicken, alongside sizzling platters, crab rangoon and kung pao chicken.
hot-pot-chen.descriptor: Chinese-American carryout on W. Stadium Blvd with clay-pot and sizzling plates

hunt-park.text: Ormond E. Hunt and his wife Maud gave the land to the city in 1943, dedicating it to Hunt's first wife, Hazel — prompted by parks superintendent Eli Gallup's request to use the ground for wartime victory gardens. First improvements came in 1953 and a shelter in 1963; Project Grow community gardens still work the site.
hunt-park.descriptor: Seven-acre hilly neighborhood park on Daniel St with downtown skyline views

huron-highlands-park.text: The city acquired this pocket park in 1960, when development of the surrounding neighborhood was approved, and began developing the park itself in 1974; path and sidewalk work followed in 2009 for ADA compliance. It's planted like a small orchard: gooseberry, raspberry and Nanking cherry shrubs, peach, apricot and pear trees west of the playground, and apple trees in a native plant garden south of it. An asphalt path links the Skydale Drive and Larkspur Street entrances.
huron-highlands-park.descriptor: 1.67-acre neighborhood park at 400 Skydale Drive with a playground and volleyball net

hyperion-coffee.text: Hyperion was founded in 2016 in Ypsilanti by Eric Mullins, Dan Kubera and Alex Merz, roasting coffee bought from small growers before demand for brewed cups pushed them out of a beans-only model. The Ann Arbor café at 111 W. Liberty opened in mid-November 2021, in the storefront Thrive Juicery had vacated — "we wanted a more intimate setting where we can have conversations with people," Mullins told the Observer.
hyperion-coffee.descriptor: Ypsilanti roaster's single-origin café at 111 W. Liberty since 2021

iggys-eggies.text: Eli Boyer, a U-M grad who also founded the Ferndale seafood bistro Voyager, started Iggy's Eggies as a walk-up window in downtown Detroit before opening this E. Liberty shop in the former Salads UP space in June 2024. The name came from his three-year-old daughter shouting for the Mario Kart character Iggy. The draw is a build-your-own egg sandwich with a runny yolk and a mustard-based house sauce.
iggys-eggies.descriptor: Custom runny-yolk egg sandwiches on E. Liberty, from Detroit, since 2024

ingalls-mall.text: The pedestrian mall is where the Ann Arbor Summer Festival stages Top of the Park — free outdoor concerts, Movies by Moonlight and street performances on the campus green.
ingalls-mall.descriptor: Campus green on Ingalls Mall, home of the Summer Festival's Top of the Park

iroquois-park.text: One of Ann Arbor's smallest parks, squeezed between houses on Iroquois Place near Stadium and Packard. The city acquired it around 1970 and it long served as "Woodbury Park Access" — a cut-through from the neighborhood to the Woodbury Gardens housing complex. Neighbors pushed to change that, and city council renamed it Iroquois Park in 2004, around when it also got its path, bench and picnic table.
iroquois-park.descriptor: Tiny pocket park with a path, bench and picnic table on Iroquois Place

island-park.text: The 5.6-acre park wraps a 1.8-acre island in the Huron River, reached by footbridges — the concrete one on the west end dates to 1918. Its Greek Revival shelter, built in 1914 by low bidder John Koch for about $860 and originally fitted with public restrooms, is the oldest shelter in the Ann Arbor park system and was designated historic by the city in the mid-1990s.
island-park.descriptor: Park on an island in the Huron River, with a 1914 Greek Revival shelter

izzys-hoagie-shop.text: Izzy's was founded by Alan Israel and bought by the Lahner family in 1989; Terry Lahner ran it for decades until his unexpected death at 52 in December 2023. Acadia Mercer, who had worked there for ten years, took over the shop, which is best known for its Philly-style cheesesteak.
izzys-hoagie-shop.descriptor: Philly-style cheesesteak and sub counter on W. Stadium Blvd.

jamaican-jerk-pit.text: Ann Arbor's Caribbean mainstay is a carry-out kitchen on S. Thayer run by native Jamaican owner Robert Campbell, who says every entree is made to order, fresh in the kitchen, and nothing is mass produced. The menu reaches past Jamaica to Trinidad and Tobago and the Bahamas, and the kitchen caters to your spice level.
jamaican-jerk-pit.descriptor: Jamaican takeout counter on S. Thayer: jerk chicken, curry, roti

jasmine.descriptor: Bubble tea café with outdoor seating near Maynard and E. William downtown

jerusalem-garden.text: Jerusalem Garden has been a downtown Ann Arbor fixture at 314 E. Liberty since 1987 and still makes its hummus the same way — by hand, every morning, from the original family recipe. Falafel is fried to order and the kabobs come off a charbroiler, with a menu that is vegetarian-, vegan- and halal-friendly.
jerusalem-garden.descriptor: Middle Eastern counter-service spot at 314 E. Liberty since 1987

joes-pizza.text: This is an outpost of Joe's Pizza, the Greenwich Village slice counter Italian immigrant Pino "Joe" Pozzuoli opened at 7 Carmine Street in 1975. The original is a New York institution for plain street-style slices; the brand has since spread beyond the city, this South University storefront among them.
joes-pizza.descriptor: New York-style slice shop on South University, outpost of NYC's Joe's

jolly-pumpkin.text: The cafe pours beer from Jolly Pumpkin Artisan Ales, the brewery Ron and Laurie Jeffries founded in Dexter in 2004 to make deliberately funky, wild-fermented ales aged in oak wine barrels, former bourbon barrels and large foudres. Its Oro de Calabaza took the 2004 gold medal in the Belgian- and French-style ale category at the Great American Beer Festival.
jolly-pumpkin.descriptor: Cafe and brewpub pouring oak-aged sour ales from Jolly Pumpkin

kanbu-sushi-downtown.text: Tiffany Kim took over the downtown Nagomi Sushi space at 241 E. Liberty when its lease came up and reopened it in December 2020 as Kanbu — Japanese for "executive" or "leader." The menu leans Japanese-Korean: build-your-own rolls wrapped in seaweed or colored soybean paper, sashimi, cupbop rice bowls, and sushi burritos stuffed with bibimbap, bulgogi or katsu.
kanbu-sushi-downtown.descriptor: Japanese-Korean sushi and rice bowls on E. Liberty since 2020

kangs.text: Kang's bills itself as a thirty-six-year-old Ann Arbor staple, which makes it one of the city's oldest Korean kitchens and a fixture of the South University strip for students and locals alike.
kangs.descriptor: Longtime home-style Korean restaurant at 1327 South University Ave

kelly-park.text: A half acre of playground, paved path and picnic table in Ann Arbor's northwest corner, near Maple Road and Miller Avenue. It takes its name from the circle of houses on nearby Kelly Green Drive, and an open field connects it to Abbot Elementary.
kelly-park.descriptor: Half-acre neighborhood playground at 1219 Patricia Ave near Maple and Miller

kelsey-museum-of-archaeology.text: Founded in 1928, the Kelsey holds more than 100,000 ancient and medieval artifacts inside Newberry Hall, a Richardsonian Romanesque building put up between 1888 and 1891. Its strength is everyday life: roughly 45,000 objects from the Roman-era Egyptian town of Karanis — the largest such collection outside Cairo — plus about 13,000 from Seleucia-on-the-Tigris in Iraq.
kelsey-museum-of-archaeology.descriptor: U-M archaeology museum in 1890s Newberry Hall on S. State St.

kempf-house-museum.text: Built in 1853, it's one of Ann Arbor's best-preserved Greek Revival houses. Music teachers Reuben and Pauline Kempf bought it in the 1890s and made it a salon, hosting Paderewski, Victor Herbert and Ernestine Schumann-Heink; their 1877 Steinway concert grand still sits in the music room. The city acquired the house in 1969 and it has been a free museum since.
kempf-house-museum.descriptor: 1853 Greek Revival house museum on S. Division St.

kimchi-box.descriptor: Korean fast-casual counter at 1771 Plymouth Rd on Ann Arbor's north side

knights-downtown-steakhouse.text: The Knight family has fed Ann Arbor since 1952, when Ray and Mary Knight bought Knight's Market on the west side. Ray added the Dexter Road steakhouse in 1984, Jackson followed in 2001, and the downtown room at Liberty and Maynard opened in 2014 — still serving beef hand-cut fresh daily at the family's own meat market.
knights-downtown-steakhouse.descriptor: Steakhouse at the corner of Liberty and Maynard, open since 2014

kosmos-bopshop.text: Don "Kosmo" Kwon closed his Kerrytown lunch counter, Kosmo's Deli, at the end of 2018 to concentrate on this S. Ashley St. spot — the "bop" in the name is bibimbap, the rice bowl he's known for. The dining room's murals were painted by Ann Arbor and Detroit graffiti artists, and the menu runs to a bacon-wrapped, deep-fried Seoul Dog.
kosmos-bopshop.descriptor: Korean rice bowls, Seoul Dogs and murals on S. Ashley St.

krazy-jims-blimpy-burger.text: Opened in 1953 by Jim Shafer on South Division, where it stayed six decades, Blimpy runs orders down a line with rules: order for yourself, don't switch places, no phones — then pick fried items, patty count (double, triple, quad or more), bun, grilled toppings and cheese as the cooks work without tickets. The university bought the old building in 2012 and Blimpy reopened on S. Ashley in September 2014. It's appeared on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives and Man v. Food.
krazy-jims-blimpy-burger.descriptor: Griddled sliders and deep-fried veggies since 1953, now on South Ashley

kuebler-langford-nature-area.text: The city bought the core of this park in 1975 from the Langford and Kuebler families, after public pressure helped sink a rezoning vote for high-rise development in 1969; later parcels brought it to 31 acres. A deep ravine bisects the park from west to east: moist woods on the steep slopes, large black and white oaks above, and native dry-prairie plants like round-headed bush clover in the old field.
kuebler-langford-nature-area.descriptor: 31-acre ravine woodland off Huron River Drive, adjoining Bird Hills

la-serre.descriptor: French brasserie in the Vanguard hotel's greenhouse-style room on Glen Ave

lab-cafe.text: lab cafe opened around 2010 on E. Liberty St. in Ann Arbor's Midtown restaurant strip, at nearly the same time as its next-door neighbor Tomukun Noodle Bar. The two owners met as new neighbors, and in June 2014 Tomukun's Thomas Yon was marrying lab cafe owner Joanna Hong.
lab-cafe.descriptor: Coffee and tea cafe on E. Liberty St. near campus

lan-city-noodle-bar.text: This is the second outpost of Lan City Noodles, whose original sits on Washtenaw Ave. in Ypsilanti; owner Soon Heng Gin opened the South University location in September 2021 in a space that had been Social House and, before that, Leo's Coney Island. The draw is Lanzhou-style noodles, hand-pulled or knife-cut, in beef-bone broth. When the Observer called, a manager said they were too short-staffed to want more customers.
lan-city-noodle-bar.descriptor: Lanzhou hand-pulled noodle bar on S. University Ave

lansdowne-park.text: The city acquired this 2.6-acre park on Lans Way, near Seventh Street in Ann Arbor's southwest corner, in 1963 as the surrounding neighborhood was developed, then built it out slowly: soccer goals in 2000, followed in 2006 by the play structure, seating, paved path and basketball upgrades. A rain garden in the northwest corner handles stormwater.
lansdowne-park.descriptor: 2.6-acre neighborhood park on Lans Way with playground and soccer field

las-vegas-park.text: Ann Arbor picked up the land around 1960 as the surrounding southwest-side neighborhood was being built out. Just under two acres running between Las Vegas Drive and Granada Avenue, it has a lit half-court, an accessible paved path, and a playground among honeylocusts and other street trees.
las-vegas-park.descriptor: Two-acre neighborhood park on Las Vegas Dr, south of Stadium Blvd

lawton-park.text: The park and the elementary school beside it are named for Uriah William Lawton (1831-1905), Ann Arbor's first school superintendent, who served from 1864 to 1867. The City of Ann Arbor and the school system bought the 12-acre site jointly and dedicated Lawton School in October 1964, deliberately pairing classrooms with public recreation land.
lawton-park.descriptor: 5-acre park with a ball diamond next to Lawton Elementary School

leslie-park.text: The city bought the 207-acre Hagen Farm from Eugene and Emily Leslie in 1963 — the largest property Ann Arbor has ever purchased for parks. The Leslies sold it on $15,000-a-year installments, then forgave the remaining debt in their wills and left a half-million-dollar trust fund on top of it. The farm became Leslie Park, the golf course, Leslie Woods and the Leslie Science Center.
leslie-park.descriptor: North-side park with ball fields, a sledding hill and a community food forest

leslie-park-golf-course.text: Ann Arbor's municipal course on Traver Road plays 6,611 yards over rolling hills — laid out by E. Lawrence Packard and later enhanced by Arthur Hills. Golf Digest has named it the #1 municipal course in Michigan, and it has also been recognized by Michigan Golfer magazine and the Michigan Golf Network.
leslie-park-golf-course.descriptor: City-run 18-hole championship course on the hills of northeast Ann Arbor

leslie-science-nature-center.text: Dr. Eugene Leslie, a University of Michigan chemical engineering professor whose property hosted pioneering work on things like no-knock gasoline, farmed this hillside with his wife Emily — Hereford cattle, hogs and orchard fruit they sold. On their deaths in 1976, months apart, they left the land to the City of Ann Arbor asking that it be used for children; their honey house is now the Critter House.
leslie-science-nature-center.descriptor: Nature center on the Leslies' former Ann Arbor farm, willed to the city for children

leslie-woods-nature-area.text: Ann Arbor bought this land in the 1960s for a traffic loop that was never built, so the woodland survived intact and now holds some of the largest trees in the park system. Natural Area Preservation staff and volunteers cut the thousand-meter trail loop in 2003; American toads, gray tree frogs and green frogs all breed here.
leslie-woods-nature-area.descriptor: 23-acre oak-hickory woods with a 1,000-meter loop below Leslie Park Golf Course

liberty-plaza.text: A 0.26-acre, two-level plaza at the corner of Liberty and Division, next to the Kempf House. Its sensory garden — plants chosen to maximize sensory impact with people with disabilities in mind, for their textures, scents, shapes and bright colors — was created in 2013 by the city's Commission on Disability Issues as a memorial to Pamela Baker Trostle, its former chair.
liberty-plaza.descriptor: Two-level quarter-acre downtown plaza at Liberty and Division

longshore-park.text: A small north-side park whose playground and picnic tables sit on top of a hill with a view of the Huron River, reached by an accessible asphalt path from the park's southeast entrance on Longshore Drive. Open grass fields and mature sugar maples and black cherries fill the rest, and Argo Park & Nature Area, Riverside Park, Beckley Park, Plymouth Parkway Park and Fairview Cemetery are all within walking distance.
longshore-park.descriptor: 2.25-acre park at 405 Longshore Drive near Argo Park & Nature Area

lowertown-bar-cafe.text: The building started life in 1938 as a mechanic's garage, and the restored, cinder-block space now works as a coffee shop by day and a cocktail bar after dark. Mornings run on Hyperion coffee roasted in Ypsilanti, plus pastries from local bakeshops; there's no on-site kitchen, so food trucks park outside most evenings, and the patio keeps fire pits going in winter.
lowertown-bar-cafe.descriptor: Coffee by day, cocktail bar by night in Ann Arbor's historic Northside

lucky-kitchen.text: Serving Plymouth Rd. since the late 1990s, Lucky Kitchen leans hard into the university crowd — it accepts U-M shortcodes for catering orders and delivers meals through Ann Arbor Meals on Wheels. It also runs an "LK Fit" menu of steamed dishes made with no oil or salt added.
lucky-kitchen.descriptor: Chinese takeout and delivery on Plymouth Rd. in Ann Arbor

m-36-coffee-roasters.text: M-36's owners, Lisa and Ken, learned the cafe trade at Espresso Royale, the Italian-inspired coffee company they came up through in the late 1980s; when it closed in the COVID-19 shutdown they bought the roasting business and launched M-36 Coffee Roasters in 2020. They roast in Whitmore Lake and pour it at this cafe at 1101 S. University.
m-36-coffee-roasters.descriptor: Roaster's cafe on S. University, with coffee roasted in Whitmore Lake

madras-masala.text: Madras Masala spent about twenty years on Maynard St. downtown until a January 20, 2023 fire, believed to have started overnight in the kitchen's ventilation system, destroyed the building. Owner Gopal Ramanujam reopened on Packard less than ten months later with South Indian and Indo-Chinese specialties — counter service now, and no more lunch buffet.
madras-masala.descriptor: South Indian and Indo-Chinese counter-service spot on Packard

madras-masala-express.text: Madras Masala spent two decades on Maynard St. downtown until a January 20, 2023 fire that started in its kitchen destroyed the building; owner Gopalsamy Ramanujam, who bought the restaurant from its founder in 2014, said he would reopen in Ann Arbor "100 percent." It came back, including this express counter on Broadway St.
madras-masala-express.descriptor: Indian restaurant on Broadway St, express offshoot of Madras Masala

maizies.descriptor: Campus cafe and market on the ground floor of the Michigan League

mama-satto.descriptor: Japanese-Korean sushi, ramen and noodle spot on N. University near campus

manchester-park.text: Acquired by the city in 1964 under the name Washtenaw-Manchester Park, this 1.5-acre strip of green between Washtenaw Avenue and Manchester Road once came with a bonus: the city also maintained the adjoining county land. That arrangement ended in 1982, when Washtenaw County took over full management of its own property as County Farm Park.
manchester-park.descriptor: 1.5-acre greenspace with a paved path beside County Farm Park

mani-osteria-and-bar.text: Mani has served Italian osteria food at 341 E. Liberty since 2011. The name is simply the Italian word for "hands" — as the restaurant puts it, "'Mani' means hands, and since 2011 ours have been busy."
mani-osteria-and-bar.descriptor: Italian osteria at 341 E. Liberty St., open since 2011

markley-dining-hall.text: The dining hall sits inside Mary Markley Hall, the 1503 Washington Heights dorm completed in 1959 for about $6.1 million and named for Mary Butler Markley, a faculty widow active in alumnae affairs. It was built to house roughly 1,000 women students and went coed in 1963, and it is one of only two dining halls serving U-M's Hill neighborhood.
markley-dining-hall.descriptor: Dining hall inside U-M's Mary Markley residence hall on the Hill

maryfield-wildwood-park.text: A 4.55-acre neighborhood park bounded by Westwood, Linwood and Maryfield, just north of Dexter Avenue — playground, half basketball court, volleyball net and a softball backstop on the west side, with a wooded ravine and trail making up the east. Wooden stairs down into the ravine from Wildwood Street carry a 2001 dedication to Bruce Folske.
maryfield-wildwood-park.descriptor: 4.5-acre west-side park with a wooded ravine, playground and ball backstop

mash.text: Mash opened on July 26, 2012 in the cellar beneath Blue Tractor, taking over the space that had been Cafe Habana's salsa-night lounge — mojitos out, bourbon and live bands in. The list runs past 70 bourbons, and all six beers on draft are brewed in-house.
mash.descriptor: Basement whiskey bar and live-music room under Blue Tractor on E. Washington

meadowbrook-park.text: Meadowbrook was developed in the late 1980s as homes were built along Northbrook Drive and at Meadowbrook Village Apartments. Its accessible paved path doubles as a shortcut, connecting the end of Seventh Street through to Northbrook Drive, and the city clears it of snow in winter.
meadowbrook-park.descriptor: 2.18-acre park at the end of S. Seventh St with a playground and half court

michigan-league.text: Built in 1929 on North University Avenue and designed by the Pond brothers, the Michigan League was the women's answer to the Michigan Union, where women had once needed a male escort and a separate north entrance. It houses the Lydia Mendelssohn Theatre; the Union's escort rule didn't fall until 1956.
michigan-league.descriptor: 1929 student union building on North University, by the Pond brothers

michigan-stadium.text: Opened in 1927 for $950,000 with 72,000 seats, Michigan Stadium now holds 107,601 — the largest stadium in the United States and third-largest in the world. Most of the bowl sits below ground level, so it looks deceptively small from the street. A record 115,109 watched Michigan play Notre Dame here in 2013, and the place has also hosted an NHL Winter Classic and a 112,000-person concert.
michigan-stadium.descriptor: College football's "Big House" — the largest stadium in the US, open since 1927

michigan-theater.text: Opened January 5, 1928 as a Lombard Romanesque movie palace, the Michigan was facing demolition when its lease ran out in 1978 until community members and organists rallied to save it. Its 1927 Barton theatre pipe organ is one of only about 45 still in their original homes and is played before screenings. The nonprofit venue hosts the Ann Arbor Film Festival.
michigan-theater.descriptor: 1928 downtown movie palace with its original Barton pipe organ
