michigans-first-jewish-cemetery-site.text: The southwest corner of E. Huron and Fletcher, now University of Michigan campus, is the site of the first Jewish cemetery in Michigan. The state designated it a Michigan historic site in 1982, and a plaque on the corner is what marks it today.
michigans-first-jewish-cemetery-site.descriptor: State historical marker at E. Huron and Fletcher on the U-M campus

mighty-good-coffee.text: Mighty Good started roasting in Ann Arbor in 2006, and its beans now turn up all over town — Argus Farm Stop, the Produce Station, Sparrow Market, Knight's. The women- and queer-run roaster moved its roasting operation out to Dexter in 2025.
mighty-good-coffee.descriptor: Local coffee roaster's cafe at 217 N. Main St., roasting since 2006

miller-nature-area.text: These 22 acres between Miller Ave. and Arborview were logged in the 1800s, then farmed, then dug as a gravel pit after 1950; the city bought the land from the Seymour and Gelman families in 1976. Unpaved trails now wind through old-field remnants and stands of big elms, and volunteers with Ann Arbor's Natural Area Preservation program have spent years clearing dumped trash and replanting natives.
miller-nature-area.descriptor: 22-acre city nature area off Miller Ave. with unpaved old-field and woods trails

minys-mexican-restaurant.text: Miny Morales started her own kitchen on Washtenaw Rd in Ypsilanti in 2017 and built the menu around her own cooking; her three sons, Fernando, Rodolfo and Rudy, all work in the business full-time, and this Lower Town location opened in 2024. Look for hand-made huaraches, squash-blossom quesadillas, pambazos, and the famously oversized "Miny burrito."
minys-mexican-restaurant.descriptor: Family-run Mexican kitchen at 1141 Broadway in Lower Town

miss-kim.text: Miss Kim is the Korean member of Zingerman's Community of Businesses in Ann Arbor. The kitchen likes to bend the canon — a cacio e pepe tteokbokki puts a southern Italian twist on the classic Korean rice-cake dish.
miss-kim.descriptor: Korean restaurant in Zingerman's Community of Businesses

mister-spots.text: Started in Bowling Green, Ohio in February 1985 by two guys named Jim, one of them a Philadelphia transplant who named the place after his cat, Spots. It was among the first restaurants in the Midwest to sell Buffalo wings; the Ann Arbor shop opened in November 1986 and still gets its Amoroso's rolls shipped in from Philadelphia.
mister-spots.descriptor: Philly cheesesteaks, hoagies and Buffalo wings on S. State since 1986

mitchell-field.text: Mitchell Field is the University of Michigan's outdoor recreation complex at 1900 Fuller Rd., between the U-M hospital and North Campus, with grass and turf fields plus sand volleyball courts. It hosts club sports and intramural games, and is open to the general public for pickup play dawn to dusk, April through November, except during scheduled events.
mitchell-field.descriptor: U-M rec fields on Fuller Rd. with sand volleyball courts

mixtwood-pomona-park.text: This under-half-acre playground at Mixtwood Street and Pomona Road, near Miller Avenue northwest of downtown Ann Arbor, holds one of the city's official Champion Trees: a pignut hickory that is the largest of its species in Ann Arbor. The current play structure, set in the shade of the park's oaks and hickories, went in during 2004, replacing an older one.
mixtwood-pomona-park.descriptor: Pocket playground at Mixtwood and Pomona, shaded by oaks and hickories

moka-and-co.text: A New York City–based chain of Yemeni coffee houses named for the port that drove the early coffee trade, Moka & Co. opened at 333 S. Main — its sixth Michigan shop — in the former Underground Printing storefront. Beans come from the cradle of coffee civilization, and the pastry case runs to Dubai chocolate: phyllo layered with pistachio spread.
moka-and-co.descriptor: Yemeni coffee house on S. Main, part of a NYC-based chain

mosher-jordan-dining-hall.text: Mosher-Jordan opened in 1930 as a residence hall named for Eliza Mosher and Myra Jordan, the University of Michigan's first two deans of women — Mosher was also the first woman the university recognized as a professor. The hall reopened in 2008 after a renovation, alongside the adjoining Hill Dining Center that serves the surrounding Hill neighborhood dorms.
mosher-jordan-dining-hall.descriptor: U-M Hill neighborhood dining hall in a 1930 residence hall

mr-yuns-tower-deli.descriptor: Korean deli counter on Fuller Ct. near the U-M medical campus

mujo-cafe.descriptor: Michigan Dining cafe in the Duderstadt Center atrium on North Campus

museum-on-main.text: The Washtenaw County Historical Society's museum occupies a house the Kellogg family built in three phases during the 1830s, around the time Michigan became a state. It originally stood on Wall St.; facing demolition, U-M donated it to the society, which moved it to N. Main in 1990 and opened it to the public in 1999. It's on the National Register and shows rotating local-history exhibits.
museum-on-main.descriptor: County historical society museum in an 1830s house, 500 N. Main

mushroom-park.text: The land was acquired in 1961 as Vernon Downs Playlot, but got its real name in 1975 when Girl Scout Troop #190 petitioned City Council: kids already called it Mushroom Park, after the concrete climbing structures built in 1962 in the shape of mushrooms. Council approved unanimously, and neighbors have since painted the mushrooms. The park also holds Ann Arbor's second-largest white oak.
mushroom-park.descriptor: 1.5-acre playlot between Waltham and Saxon, named for its concrete mushrooms

nagomi-sushi.text: Nick Ma opened Nagomi in mid-December 2009 in the old Bagel Fragel space at Plymouth View Center, the fourth sushi restaurant to arrive in Ann Arbor that year. The room seats 37, eight of them at the sushi bar. A downtown offshoot he opened on E. Liberty in December 2015 passed to his cousin Tiffany Kim in December 2020 and was renamed Kanbu Sushi.
nagomi-sushi.descriptor: Sushi restaurant at Plymouth View Center on Plymouth Rd since 2009

namaste-flavours.descriptor: Indian restaurant on S. Division serving South Indian dishes

native-american-land-gift.text: The plaque marks an 1817 land grant made through the Treaty of Fort Meigs, in which the Ojibwa, Odawa and Potawatomi gave land to benefit Catholic education under Fr. Gabriel Richard and the college at Detroit. Those lands were later sold to benefit the University of Michigan, which moved to Ann Arbor in 1837. U-M's History and Traditions Committee placed the marker in 2001 as Site #8.
native-american-land-gift.descriptor: 1817 land-grant plaque on the University of Michigan campus, installed 2001

nelson-meade-county-farm-park.text: Washtenaw County has owned this ground since 1836, when it bought 141 acres from Claudius Britton, and from 1837 it was the county poor farm — later the Washtenaw Infirmary, which closed in 1971 and was demolished in 1979. Project Grow began gardening eight acres here in 1972 and it remains the oldest and largest site in its network. The county renamed the park in 2013 for Nelson Meade, who served on its parks commission for more than 40 years.
nelson-meade-county-farm-park.descriptor: 141-acre county park with trails and Project Grow community garden plots

new-york-pizza-depot.text: Known around campus as NYPD, it was opened in 1997 by cousins Mauro and Domenico Telemaco, who had run a pizza restaurant in New York before coming to Ann Arbor. The family later franchised the New York-style pies cautiously under the name Uncle D's: "The main goal is not to open up like mushrooms," partner Maurizio Grillo said. "Most people hear 'franchise' and they think it's some big corporation, but this is just small, just our family."
new-york-pizza-depot.descriptor: New York-style pizza near the U-M campus since 1997

newport-creek-nature-area.text: This one-acre pocket of woods on Ann Arbor's far northwest side has no established trails at all — the city explicitly encourages off-trail exploration. The land came to the city from the neighborhood's developer under a 1998 development agreement, the same deal that produced nearby Riverwood Nature Area, and crews are still working to clear out non-native invasive plants.
newport-creek-nature-area.descriptor: One-acre trail-free wooded nature area west of Newport Road, northwest Ann Arbor

nichols-arboretum.text: Founded in 1907 after Esther and Walter Nichols donated their 27-acre farm to the university, the Arb was laid out by landscape architect O.C. Simonds, whose "long views" still run out to tree-filled horizons from the Main Valley. Its W.E. Upjohn Peony Garden holds roughly 350 cultivars — the largest heirloom peony collection in North America — and Shakespeare in the Arb has staged plays across the grounds since 2000.
nichols-arboretum.descriptor: 128-acre arboretum by the Huron River, "the Arb," with a huge heirloom peony garden

nickels-arcade.text: Tom E. Nickels had this covered arcade built between 1915 and 1918 on State Street land assembled from his grandfather's meat market site, in a form popularized by the Cleveland Arcade. Herman Pipp designed it, with a wire-glass gable skylight over the 261-foot gallery; the Farmers and Mechanics Bank was the first tenant in 1915, and it is thought to be Michigan's only surviving freestanding commercial arcade.
nickels-arcade.descriptor: Glass-roofed 1918 shopping arcade off S. State Street

no-thai.text: No Thai! opened on September 25, 2005 in a 675-square-foot storefront and grew into six Michigan locations, five of them in Ann Arbor — by the owners' own rough count, about 8.5 million dishes later. The Plymouth Road shop at 1745 Plymouth Rd. is the Northside outpost.
no-thai.descriptor: Thai-inspired counter on Plymouth Rd., the Northside No Thai!

no-thai-bryant-pattengill-east.text: The name comes from the head chef: four friends made a pact in February 2005 to bring a modern Thai restaurant to the community, and when Noerung "No" Hang rose to become head chef it became "No Thai!". It opened that September 25 in a tiny 675-square-foot space and now runs several Ann Arbor storefronts plus Brighton — this South Industrial address is the delivery operation.
no-thai-bryant-pattengill-east.descriptor: Delivery kitchen for Ann Arbor's No Thai! chain, on S. Industrial Hwy

no-thai-burns-park.text: The Ann Arbor-born chain takes its name from head chef Noerung "No" Hang and opened its first 675-square-foot store on September 25, 2005; it now lists six Michigan locations after its East Lansing outpost closed in May 2025. This is the South U store at 1300 S. University Ave.
no-thai-burns-park.descriptor: Thai fast-casual counter on South University Ave at the edge of campus

no-thai-kerrytown.text: No Thai! opened on September 25, 2005 in a 675-square-foot Ann Arbor storefront and is named for head chef Noerung "No" Hang. The founders estimate they've cooked roughly 8.5 million dishes since, across six Michigan locations; this one sits at 226 N. Fourth Ave. in Kerrytown, just south of the farmers market.
no-thai-kerrytown.descriptor: Thai fast-casual on N. Fourth Ave in Kerrytown, Ann Arbor mini-chain since 2005

north-main-park.text: Half an acre of tall trees just north of downtown, and really a shortcut as much as a park — its accessible paved path connects N. Main Street through to N. Fourth Avenue, and the city clears it of snow in winter. Ann Arbor bought the lot in 1976 for $9,360 and paved the paths the following year; a group of neighbors keeps up the small garden on the east side.
north-main-park.descriptor: Half-acre shaded pocket park linking N. Main St to N. Fourth Ave

north-quad-dining-hall.text: The dining hall anchors North Quadrangle, which opened in fall 2010. The University of Michigan built it as a marketplace-style dining center rather than a single cafeteria line, alongside modern student rooms, a high-tech media gateway, classrooms and seminar spaces, and lounges on each floor.
north-quad-dining-hall.descriptor: Marketplace-style dining hall in North Quad, opened in fall 2010

north-star-lounge.text: Phillis Engelbert of Detroit Street Filling Station opened North Star in October 2022 at Fifth and Catherine. The all-vegan bar — billed as Michigan's only one — fills an 1887 building that started life as a horse stable and most recently housed a day spa; the upstairs room hosts live music five nights a week, with themed nights for Hot Club jazz, piano bar and bluegrass.
north-star-lounge.descriptor: All-vegan bar and live-music venue at 301 N. Fifth Ave., opened 2022

northeast-tower-tisch.text: The tower marks the northeast corner of Michigan Stadium, which opened in 1927 and now seats 107,601 — the largest stadium in the United States and the Western Hemisphere, and the third largest in the world.
northeast-tower-tisch.descriptor: Corner tower at the northeast end of Michigan Stadium, the Big House

northside-grill.text: Jim Koli has run this Broadway St. diner since 1993, and weekend breakfast lines routinely stretch down the block. The building once housed the Cloverleaf Dairy, and vintage dairy photographs still hang on the walls.
northside-grill.descriptor: Broadway St. breakfast diner in a former Cloverleaf Dairy, open since 1993

northside-park.text: The land came out of the old Northside School site and was designated for public park use in 1939; the shelter followed in 1960 and the tennis and basketball courts in 1982. The adjoining CAN Northside Community Center went solar in 2020, becoming the city's first "resilience hub" — able to keep refrigeration and power running during an outage.
northside-park.descriptor: 5.2-acre park at Pontiac Trail and Taylor St with ball diamonds and a rec center

northwest-tower-ross.text: One of the brick corner towers of Michigan Stadium — the Big House. Its official capacity, 107,601, has carried one unexplained "extra" seat since 1956, said to belong to coach Fritz Crisler; nobody knows which seat it is. A record 115,109 crowded in for Notre Dame in September 2013.
northwest-tower-ross.descriptor: Corner tower of Michigan Stadium, the 107,601-seat Big House

oakridge-nature-area.text: Eight acres of oak-hickory woods on Glazier Way with no trails, no amenities and no parking on site — you walk or bike in from Huron Parkway, or park on Wolverhampton Lane five minutes away. The city counts over 100 native species here, and Miller Creek runs through alongside a small fen, which the city calls a rare type of Michigan wetland.
oakridge-nature-area.descriptor: Eight acres of trail-free oak-hickory woods on Glazier Way

old-town-tavern.text: Open since 1972 at 122 W. Liberty, the Old Town started as a blue-collar bar that opened at 6 a.m. to accommodate third-shift workers from area factories. It calls itself one of downtown Ann Arbor's most beloved townie bars.
old-town-tavern.descriptor: Townie bar at 122 W. Liberty, established 1972

onder-park.text: The city bought these 4.2 acres of north-side woods in 2007 from Jan Onder, a local businesswoman who had owned the land with her late husband Ned Shure since 1992; it had been appraised at $480,000 two years earlier. Two small streams and many pockets of wooded wetland make it a green corridor, with trillium and marsh marigolds in the spring.
onder-park.descriptor: 4.2-acre wooded nature area with unpaved trails off Brookside Drive

one-bowl.descriptor: Asian rice-bowl shop on South University in the campus block

pacific-rim.text: Pacific Rim grew out of Kana, a Korean restaurant Mr. and Mrs. Ko opened near the U-M hospital in 1982; it moved downtown in 1995. In 2000 their son Y.B. Ko took over and partnered with Duc Tang — Saigon-born, a Yale biochemistry grad with no formal culinary training — to push the menu pan-Asian, and Duc has run it alone since Y.B. left for Hawaii in 2007. He rejects the word "fusion."
pacific-rim.descriptor: Upscale pan-Asian restaurant in downtown Ann Arbor

palace-tang.text: Palace Tang, named for the Tang dynasty that ruled imperial China from the seventh through ninth centuries, opened in May 2024 in a former Panera Bread on Plymouth Rd. Thirty imported tables let diners pick one to four broths and cook their own meat, seafood and noodles; the menu lists items like "one meter fat cow" and "fish roe lucky bag."
palace-tang.descriptor: Chinese hot pot on Plymouth Rd., in the old Panera space

palio.text: Palio has been on S. Main since September 1991, named for the bareback horse race run through Siena — the winners of that race are recorded on a mural in the back dining room. In summer the rooftop, Palio Del Sole, runs its own kitchen and a menu completely different from downstairs, plus sangria by the pitcher.
palio.descriptor: Italian trattoria at 347 S. Main with a seasonal rooftop bar, since 1991

palmer-house.text: Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Usonian house in 1950 for U-M economics professor William Palmer and his wife Mary, and it was built in 1952 from red cypress and brick on a triangular grid with no right angles in the structure. The Palmer family owned it until 2009; it joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1999.
palmer-house.descriptor: 1952 Frank Lloyd Wright Usonian house near Nichols Arboretum

panda-house.text: Owner Eric Cheng, who is from Fujian province, has run Panda House in Maple Village since about 2005, and in 2015 opened a second Ann Arbor restaurant, Chopsticks, with largely the same menu. It serves the American-Chinese standards plus pad Thai — made, Cheng told the Ann Arbor Observer, with the same noodles as the Fujian noodle soup he grew up on, which isn't on the menu here.
panda-house.descriptor: Chinese restaurant in the Maple Village shopping center, owner-run since ~2005

paris-bahn-mi.text: The former owners of the Ding Tea boba shop on E. William expanded into the storefront next door and opened Paris Banh Mi there — a remodeled 3,700-square-foot cafe seating 72. Banh mi come on fresh-baked baguettes and croissants, alongside pho, Korean corn dogs, egg rolls and bubble tea.
paris-bahn-mi.descriptor: Vietnamese-French bakery and banh mi cafe on E. William

peony-garden.text: William E. Upjohn, a U-M medical alumnus, donated his personal peony collection to the Arb in 1922, and the garden opened in 1927 with 280 cultivars. About 196 of those originals still grow among roughly 350 cultivars today — the largest public collection of heirloom, pre-1950 herbaceous peonies in North America. Peak bloom is late May into early June.
peony-garden.descriptor: Heirloom peony garden in Nichols Arboretum; blooms late May–early June

pilars-tamales.text: Sylvia Nolasco-Rivers has been feeding Ann Arbor Salvadoran tamales and pupusas for more than twenty years, having moved her family here and grown the restaurant out of catering work. Her fundraising for causes back in El Salvador grew into Pilar's Foundation, incorporated as a nonprofit in 2019.
pilars-tamales.descriptor: Salvadoran tamales and pupusas on W Liberty St, run by its founder

pioneer-woods-nature-area.text: The woods and the adjoining Greenview meadow are owned by Ann Arbor Public Schools and managed by the City of Ann Arbor together with the volunteer Friends of Greenview, a nonprofit that has been at work here for more than twenty years planting native trees and restoring meadow, woodland and pond habitat. More than 50 butterfly species have been recorded on the site.
pioneer-woods-nature-area.descriptor: Volunteer-restored woods, meadow and pond stewarded by Friends of Greenview

pita-kabob-grill.text: A small counter-service Mediterranean shop at 619 E. William, a block off central campus, built around made-to-order shawarma, grilled kabobs, pita wraps and falafel. The menu leans Lebanese, and it keeps student-friendly late hours six days a week, closing entirely on Sundays.
pita-kabob-grill.descriptor: Counter-service Mediterranean shawarma and kabob shop on E. William St

pita-king.descriptor: Middle Eastern pita and shawarma counter on E. Stadium Blvd

pizza-bobs.text: An Ann Arbor rite of passage since 1972, best known for the Original Chipati — trademarked, house sauce and all — alongside thick milkshakes, toasted subs and pizza. It has fed more than fifty years of students on the State Street strip; the shop's own site dates the Chipati itself to 1971.
pizza-bobs.descriptor: Pizza, toasted subs and the original Chipati at 800 S. State since 1972

pizza-house.descriptor: Campus-area pizzeria on Church Street near South University

pizza-pazza.text: Pizza Pazza started as a wood-fired food truck before growing into a permanent home inside Kerrytown Market & Shops. The kitchen keeps to Neapolitan rules — poolish-fermented dough fired at 900 degrees in about three minutes, and a sauce that is plum tomatoes, olive oil and sea salt, nothing more.
pizza-pazza.descriptor: Wood-fired Neapolitan pizzeria inside Kerrytown Market on N. Fifth Ave

plate-sushi-chicken.text: Jane Kim opened the Japanese restaurant M Totoro on S. State in 2003, sold it in 2008 to focus on family, then returned to the business in December 2021 with Plate, run with her friend Esther Kim. It took over Lower Town's former Yourist Studio Gallery and pairs sushi and bento boxes with Korean fried chicken.
plate-sushi-chicken.descriptor: Sushi and Korean fried chicken on Broadway in Lower Town

plymouth-parkway-park.text: The city got these six acres in 1927 as a gift from the Washtenaw County Board of Road Commissioners, deeded for park use only. It straddles both sides of Plymouth Road near the Broadway and Maiden Lane junction, with Traver Creek and mature shade trees along the southern edge; the playground was added in 2004.
plymouth-parkway-park.descriptor: Six-acre park along Traver Creek where Plymouth Rd meets Broadway

poke-poke.text: Poke Poke landed at 312 S. State St. in 2019 — the fifth poke place to open in Ann Arbor inside a single year — as an outpost of a Southfield-based chain that now lists a dozen Michigan locations plus three in the Tampa area. The pitch is "sushi unrolled": one build-your-own counter, vegan and gluten-free items labeled on the menu, and basement seating students use for studying.
poke-poke.descriptor: Build-your-own poke bowls at 312 S. State St. near North University

pollinator-garden.text: A volunteer-built demonstration garden just east of the Project Grow site in Greenview Nature Area, expanded to a quarter acre in 2022 and planted over several years with more than 200 native wildflower plugs and grasses. The neighbor-run Friends of Greenview and Pioneer Nature Area have documented more than 50 butterfly species in the park and have used goats to knock back invasive plants.
pollinator-garden.descriptor: Quarter-acre native-plant demonstration garden at Greenview Nature Area

postmans-rest-park.text: The park is named for mail carriers Norm Kern and Bob Schlupe, who regularly checked on Anne B. Mueller, an elderly widow living alone on this wooded lot. After she died in 1965 at 85, neighbor and city council member Margaret D. Towsley helped arrange the land's donation, and the park was dedicated in June 1966 to "the unselfish mail carriers throughout the years who have devoted so much time in the service of others."
postmans-rest-park.descriptor: Small wooded pocket park at Wayne St and Vinewood Blvd with a swinging bench

pretzel-bell.text: The original Pretzel Bell ran from 1934 to 1985 at 120 E. Liberty, a gathering place for townies and students where celebrations meant ringing the house bell and the Michigan Daily staff, the Men's Glee Club and bluegrass band the RFD Boys were regulars. The name was revived at 226 S. Main, where the P-Bell still trades on that U-M history.
pretzel-bell.descriptor: U-M-themed bar and grill at 226 S. Main

professors-monument.text: A half-broken limestone column on a low pedestal at the southeast corner of the Hatcher Graduate Library — the snapped shaft is the old symbol for a life cut short. Its plaques honor early U-M professors, among them Douglass Houghton, Michigan's first state geologist and the "father of copper mining," who drowned in Lake Superior in 1845 at 36.
professors-monument.descriptor: Broken-column memorial at the SE corner of Hatcher Graduate Library

project-grow-gardens.text: Project Grow has run organic community gardens in Ann Arbor since 1972, and now manages roughly two dozen sites and more than 350 plots around the city. This one sits on the Leslie Science & Nature Center grounds and has 37 raised beds.
project-grow-gardens.descriptor: Community garden plots at Leslie Science & Nature Center

q-bakehouse-market.text: Rachel Liu Martindale trained as an engineer before turning a baking side project, Milk + Honey, run with her husband Jonathan, into Q Bakehouse & Market at 1608 Jackson Ave. The name is a Taiwanese term for chewy, springy texture, and the counter is known for savory cheddar and chili-crisp scones, milk-bread buns, whipped cream cakes and frozen dumplings.
q-bakehouse-market.descriptor: Asian-inspired bakery and market on Jackson Ave.

quickly.text: Quickly is the American arm of Taiwan's Kuai Ke Li tapioca-milk-tea franchise, founded by Nancy Yang and now past 2,000 stores worldwide. The U.S. side launched in California in 1996 and marketed itself as an Asian-fusion cafe rather than a plain boba stand, later adding frozen yogurt and Hong Kong-style egg puffs.
quickly.descriptor: Taiwanese bubble tea cafe on S. University Ave

rappourt.text: Rappourt took over the Plymouth Road Mall space that had long been the Wine Seller, reopening in 2017 as a north-side pub built around forty-some beers and communal tables. The Ann Arbor Observer found a menu wandering from kung pao wings to moussaka lasagnette, though the bartender's summary was simpler: "This is a bar in Michigan, so basically we serve burgers."
rappourt.descriptor: Family-owned gastropub with 36 rotating taps in the Plymouth Road Mall

ray-fisher-stadium.text: It's named for Ray Fisher, who left the Cincinnati Reds after the 1920 season to coach Michigan and was ruled ineligible for leaving without proper notice — Commissioner Landis upheld the complaint, and Bowie Kuhn didn't reinstate him until 1980. Fisher coached here 38 seasons, winning 15 Big Ten titles and the 1953 College World Series.

real-seafood-company.text: Founder Dennis opened Real Seafood Co. in 1975 on the bet that downtown Ann Arbor needed a proper fish house to match the character Main Street was building; it was an instant hit and has held the corner for five decades. The room still runs an oyster bar and three-season open-air atria over the sidewalk, and the name has since spread to Toledo, Bay City, Grand Rapids and Coconut Point, Florida.
real-seafood-company.descriptor: Seafood house and oyster bar at 341 S. Main St. since 1975

recess-cafe.text: Recess calls itself a "third place" for parents: a full children's play area attached to a cafe with a light menu, wine, beer and non-alcoholic drinks. The idea is that having kids doesn't mean you have to sacrifice going out — regulars also use it to work remotely or host parties and events, and walk-ins are welcome.
recess-cafe.descriptor: Cafe with a children's play area serving coffee, beer and wine

revive.text: Revive and its twin mini-market Replenish bookend the Zaragon Place student high-rise at 619 E. University, a spinoff from the Red Hawk's owners built as a love letter to local suppliers — Zingerman's Bakehouse bread, Mighty Good coffee. There's no door from the building's lobby, so residents have to go out the front door and come in from the street.
revive.descriptor: Sandwich cafe paired with the Replenish mini-market at Zaragon on E. University

ricewood.text: Ricewood started in 2015 as a barbecue truck parked behind Morgan & York, run by chef Frank Fejeran and his brother Gabe Golub, who spent a winter working for free at a Texas barbecue joint to learn smoking. The Maple Village storefront opened in early May 2022 — their first independent location — serving brisket and pulled pork over rice with finadene, the soy-vinegar sauce from Fejeran's Guamanian side.
ricewood.descriptor: Texas-style BBQ rice bowls at Maple Village since 2022

ricewood-bbq.text: Frank Fejeran left a chef's job at the Ravens Club and started Ricewood in 2015 as a barbecue truck in the lot behind Morgan & York on Packard, with his brother Gabe Golub; in 2019 it moved indoors at the renamed York. The bowls are smoked meat over rice with finadene, a vinegar-soy sauce with tomato and scallion drawn from Fejeran's Guamanian heritage.
ricewood-bbq.descriptor: Barbecue rice bowls with Guam finadene, inside York on Packard

rich-j-c.text: A South University fixture for Korean home cooking: kimchi jjigae, dolsot bibimbap and seafood soon tofu. Regulars knew the founding couple only as Ajumma and Ahjussi. They retired and sold the place at the end of April 2023, and it has carried on under new ownership.
rich-j-c.descriptor: Longtime Korean home-cooking restaurant on South University Ave

ricks-american-cafe.text: Rick's has been a University of Michigan student fixture at 611 Church Street since 1980, running DJs and a dance floor most nights and showing Michigan and Michigan State games. The Daily Meal named it one of the 25 best college bars in America.
ricks-american-cafe.descriptor: College bar and DJ dance spot on Church Street since 1980

riverside-park.text: The land was an unofficial dump before parks superintendent Eli Gallup assembled it from sixteen separate parcels between 1925 and 1934; Depression-era WPA crews cleaned it up and the playground was completed in 1934. A grove of redbud trees here is dedicated to veterans of World War I, and the Border-to-Border Trail runs through on its way to Argo and Island parks.
riverside-park.descriptor: 15-acre Huron River park off Canal St with a WWI redbud grove

riverwood-nature-area.text: This upland forest remnant exists because it was negotiated into the Newport Ridge Subdivision development plan in 1998, leaving 4.82 acres inside a condo neighborhood. One short trail runs past a central mound and a wetland with a small stream, under oaks and hickories, with dogwood, buttonbush, turtlehead and spring wildflowers. It doubles as a green buffer between the residential area and the highway.
riverwood-nature-area.descriptor: 4.8-acre remnant forest on Riverwood Drive, a green buffer along M-14

roosroast-coffee.text: RoosRoast has been roasting in Ann Arbor since 2005 — "born in a garage, raised in Ann Arbor," as it puts it — and is known nearly as much for its blend names as its beans: Lobster Butter Love, Rich French Neighbor, A-A Cowboy.
roosroast-coffee.descriptor: Ann Arbor coffee roaster and café, born in a garage in 2005

sadako.text: Sadako has been a family-owned Japanese restaurant on South University since 2005, feeding the campus crowd sushi and cooked Japanese dishes. It's walk-in only — no reservations — and dine-in orders come with complimentary soup and salad.
sadako.descriptor: Family-owned Japanese restaurant on South University Ave since 2005

saica.text: Saica has fed the Plymouth Road side of town since 1998 from a small storefront under three orange awnings in a courtyard of one-story shops, mixing Japanese and Korean cooking — sushi rolls next to curry udon, gyoza and seaweed salad. Owner You Na's stated rule: she'll only serve customers food she would feed her own kids.
saica.descriptor: Japanese-Korean sushi and noodle spot on Plymouth Rd, open since 1998

savas.text: Sava Lelcaj opened a 24-seat cafe on State St. in 2007; when Zanzibar across the street closed in 2009 she moved into its space and expanded to 300 seats. Now Sava Farah, she has built the Pulpo Group around it, which also runs Aventura, the Dixboro Project and Orijin Bakery.
savas.descriptor: All-day restaurant and brunch spot at 216 S. State St.

scorekeepers.descriptor: Campus sports bar at 310 Maynard St.

sculpture-plaza.text: This small plaza on the seam between downtown Ann Arbor and Kerrytown is anchored by the Kerrytown Arch, an 18-foot corten-steel sculpture by David Heberling erected in 1977 with a Michigan Council for the Arts grant and restored in 2007–08 after graffiti damage. Picnic tables, seating and bike racks sit beneath it, and the People's Food Co-op tends two large gardens here through the city's Adopt-a-Park program.
sculpture-plaza.descriptor: Pocket park at 230 N. Fourth Ave. under the 18-foot Kerrytown Arch

seva.text: Steve Bellock and Barney Greenbaum started Seva Longevity Cookery in Columbus in 1971; Bellock moved to Ann Arbor in 1973 and turned the Soybean Cellars restaurant — in a former VFW hall on E. Liberty — into Seva, an all-vegetarian menu at a time that was nearly unheard of. Head cook Maren Jackson and her husband Jeff bought it in 1997, and in 2014 it left downtown for Westgate at Jackson and Maple.
seva.descriptor: Vegetarian restaurant at Westgate on Jackson Ave., in Ann Arbor since 1973

shalimar.descriptor: North Indian, Mughlai and tandoori cooking at 307 S. Main St.

side-biscuit.text: Jordan Balduf started Side Biscuit out of his own driveway in spring 2020, built a following at pop-ups around Ann Arbor and Michigan, and then took a permanent shop on Packard Street. The namesake side — the Weckscuit — is a buttermilk drop biscuit with caraway and smoked sea salt, served with horseradish crema.
side-biscuit.descriptor: Wing shop on Packard St with its namesake buttermilk biscuits

slurping-turtle.text: Chef Takashi Yagihashi — a Top Chef Masters fan favorite whose Chicago original took a Michelin Bib Gourmand in 2013 — brought Slurping Turtle from Chicago to E. Liberty in spring 2014. The noodles are made in house, and the turtle in the name is a Japanese symbol of longevity and good luck.
slurping-turtle.descriptor: Japanese ramen and sushi on E. Liberty from chef Takashi Yagihashi

songbird-cafe.text: Jenny Song's original Songbird Café on Plymouth Rd. was an instant success even with a Starbucks nearby, which pushed her to open a smaller second Songbird on Jackson Ave. in 2015 — "something smaller, where we could edit down our menu." The west-side spinoff closed in June 2021 for staffing shortages and reopened in February 2022; the Plymouth Rd. original never closed.
songbird-cafe.descriptor: Breakfast-and-lunch cafe on Plymouth Rd with espresso and baked goods

sottinis-sub-shop.text: Sottini's has been family owned since 1980 and works out of a downtown storefront on S. Fourth Ave, with a menu of twenty-plus cold and hot subs built on hand-sliced meat.
sottinis-sub-shop.descriptor: Family-run sub shop on S. Fourth Ave downtown since 1980

south-maple-park.text: The eastern two acres were bought in 1976 with money from a 1971 park bond issue, serving nearby housing complexes that had no park within walking distance. The tennis courts — now over-striped for pickleball — went in in 1979, built on top of a water reservoir that gave a large flat area to work with.
south-maple-park.descriptor: Tennis and pickleball courts with open fields off W. Liberty Street

south-quad-dining-hall.text: South Quad opened in 1951 as one of Michigan's big Central Campus residence halls. It reopened for the fall 2014 term after extensive renovations that added an all-new dining facility built around 10 unique restaurant concepts, alongside music practice rooms, a new community center, redesigned group study rooms and air conditioning.
south-quad-dining-hall.descriptor: U-M dining hall inside the South Quad residence hall on Central Campus

south-university-park.text: Two abandoned houses stood on this lot until neighbors — chiefly Leslie and Michael Morris — led a community effort to turn it into park space; the city acquired the property in the early 1970s. Michael Morris went on to serve on City Council from 1977 to 1983, and a $50,000 gift from the Morris family helped fund the park's roughly $43,000 renovation in 2012–13.
south-university-park.descriptor: Half-acre pocket park with a shaded half-court at S. University and Walnut

spencer.text: Steve Hall and Abby Olitzky opened Spencer in October 2015, funded by a $33,000 Kickstarter, and renamed it from 'Central Provisions' to avoid confusion with a Portland, Maine restaurant of that name. The downtown restaurant and cheese bar was a 2025 James Beard Award semifinalist for Outstanding Wine and Other Beverages Program.
spencer.descriptor: Restaurant and cheese bar at 113 E. Liberty in downtown Ann Arbor, since 2015

spiedo.text: Brad Greenhill — a Cleveland-born U-M engineering grad turned self-taught chef, best known for the acclaimed Detroit restaurant Takoi — opened Spiedo in September 2023 after delays from equipment supply-chain trouble, break-ins and DIY general contracting. Nearly everything comes off two vertical rotisseries and a griddle, about half the menu is vegetarian, and the space was Chela's before he took it.
spiedo.descriptor: "Mediterranean-ish" rotisserie and griddle at 307 S. Fifth Ave., opened 2023

stapp-nature-area.text: This 8-acre stand of mature oak and hickory off Huron Parkway is named for Dr. William B. Stapp, the U-M professor who founded the university's Environmental Education program and led it from 1970 to 1993, and who created the Global Rivers Environmental Education Network. Rustic trails link three trailheads, and a small vernal pool fills for frogs and toads.
stapp-nature-area.descriptor: Eight-acre oak-hickory woods with rustic trails off Huron Parkway

stars-cafe.descriptor: Middle Eastern cafe on Jackson Ave — shawarma, falafel, hummus

sunset-brooks-nature-area.text: In 2002 developers proposed 33 condominiums on this hillside. Neighbors formed the Greater Sunset Brooks Neighborhood Association and 96 contributors raised more than $93,000 toward buying the land, and the city completed the purchase in 2003. The oak-hickory woods hold a grove of flowering dogwoods and uncommon plants like redbud, wild black currant, summer grape and golden alexander.
sunset-brooks-nature-area.descriptor: 7.8 acres of woods and wetland on Sunset Road, a shortcut to Bird Hills

sweetwaters-coffee-tea.text: Wei and Lisa Bee founded the first Sweetwaters in downtown Ann Arbor in 1993, near their alma mater, pairing classic café fare with globally influenced coffees and teas. The brand has since franchised well beyond Michigan, and the founders remain part of daily life in the stores.
sweetwaters-coffee-tea.descriptor: Coffee and tea house at 123 W. Washington St.; Ann Arbor-born since 1993

writtenFor.name: Sweetwater's Coffee & Tea - Old West Side

sweetwaters-coffee-tea-kerrytown.text: Wei and Lisa Bee, who both attended the University of Michigan, opened the first Sweetwaters downtown in 1993 and grew it into a small chain built on classic cafe fare and globally influenced coffees and teas. The Kerrytown shop sits in the Kerrytown Market & Shops beside the farmers market, and is the only Ann Arbor location the company flags as serving alcohol.
sweetwaters-coffee-tea-kerrytown.descriptor: Coffee and tea cafe in Kerrytown Market & Shops; Ann Arbor born, 1993

sweetwaters-coffee-tea-old-west-side.text: This Sweetwaters pours inside the Ann Arbor District Library's Westgate branch, which reopened in September 2016 with what the library bills as the first full-service cafe in an AADL building. The chain itself is homegrown: U-M alumni Wei and Lisa Bee opened the first Sweetwaters downtown in 1993.
sweetwaters-coffee-tea-old-west-side.descriptor: Coffeehouse inside the library's Westgate branch on Jackson Ave

taq-taqueria-restaurant-bar.text: Cynthia Gagalis Messmore opened it as La Taqueria in 2018 at 106 E. Liberty with just eight tables and a half-dozen barstools; it has since moved into the original Pretzel Bell building at Liberty and S. Fourth and more than quadrupled its seating, and a Tribeca offshoot followed in 2023. Her son Mark: "Just because they're tacos doesn't mean it has to be Mexican food."
taq-taqueria-restaurant-bar.descriptor: Gourmet taco and margarita bar in downtown Ann Arbor's Pretzel Bell building

taste-of-india-suvai.text: Two former Northwest Airlines employees from Chennai, Mohana Krishnalal and Lakshmanan Muthu, opened a restaurant called Suvai in Livonia in 2004, then brought it to Ann Arbor in July 2010 — 'suvai' means taste in Tamil. They took over the S. State St. storefront that had been Kaleidoscope for 18 years and started from, as Krishnalal put it, 'four walls, and that's it.' Dosas and an Indian/Indo-Chinese lunch buffet are the draw.
taste-of-india-suvai.descriptor: South Indian dosas and lunch buffet at 217 S. State St. since 2010

teahaus.text: Lisa McDonald opened TeaHaus in Kerrytown after years in Europe designing a tea sommelier training program for a German company, and the shop now stocks more than 200 loose-leaf teas; she co-wrote "Tea for Dummies" in 2022. After extensive renovations that same year it reopened as a Tea Bar and Lounge stocked with books, games and puzzles to nudge people toward conversation.
teahaus.descriptor: Kerrytown tea shop and tea bar with 200+ loose-leaf teas

the-ark.text: Four Ann Arbor churches started the Ark in 1965 as a campus coffeehouse — a warm, safe place free from drugs and alcohol — in a house on Hill Street; Iggy Pop (then drummer James Osterberg), Gilda Radner and Will Geer all turned up in its early rooms. It moved to South Main Street in 1984, settled at 316 S. Main in 1996, and in 2012 bought its venue as a condominium, the first space it has owned.
the-ark.descriptor: Nonprofit folk music club at 316 S. Main, running since 1965

the-black-pearl.text: Open at 302 S. Main since 2008 under Harry and Jan Cohen, Black Pearl made its name on contemporary interpretations of classic seafood, with a sushi chef working alongside the kitchen. Heated greenhouse dining out front lets the outdoor seats stay in use through a Michigan winter.
the-black-pearl.descriptor: Seafood and sushi restaurant on S. Main St downtown, open since 2008

the-blind-pig-8-ball-saloon.text: Opened in 1971 as a European-influenced cafe pairing espresso with blues, and named by its founders for Prohibition-era speakeasies, the Blind Pig became Ann Arbor's rock room: Nirvana sold out the 400-capacity space in 1989, and Soundgarden, Pearl Jam and Sonic Youth all played it. Roy and Betty Goffett took over in 1982, expanded the building and opened the 8 Ball Saloon on the lower level.
the-blind-pig-8-ball-saloon.descriptor: Live-music club at 208 S. First St. since 1971, with the 8 Ball Saloon downstairs

the-brown-jug.text: The Jug is named for the Little Brown Jug, the oldest trophy in college football, and bills itself as Ann Arbor's original game-day headquarters, open since 1936. Its sandwiches are named for Michigan greats — Harbaugh's Famous Brown Jug Burger, Charles Woodson's patty melt, Bo Schembechler's boursin melt and Dylan Larkin's super hoagie.
the-brown-jug.descriptor: Michigan sports bar at 1204 S. University named for the Little Brown Jug trophy

the-cellar-at-grizzly-peak.text: The Cellar sits in the lower level of the old Del Rio Bar building at Washington and Ashley — a legendary Ann Arbor hangout whose Ashley Street wall now carries a Brian Whitfield mural honoring Thelonious Monk, though readers wrote the Observer to say Monk almost certainly never played in Ann Arbor at all.
the-cellar-at-grizzly-peak.descriptor: Lower-level bar under Grizzly Peak Brewing at Washington and Ashley

the-chop-house.text: The Chop House is the white-tablecloth steakhouse of the local Main Street Ventures group — the same family as Gratzi, Palio, Real Seafood Co. and Carson's — serving USDA prime beef and seafood in a historic Main Street building with an adjoining leather-furnished cigar lounge.
the-chop-house.descriptor: Prime-beef steakhouse at 322 S. Main with a cigar lounge

the-diag.text: The oldest part of the University of Michigan campus, it was originally the "Diagonal Green" and takes its nickname from the diagonal sidewalks cutting across it. It has long been the campus's rally and protest ground, and in 2008 spring commencement was moved here while Michigan Stadium was under construction.
the-diag.descriptor: Central-campus green crossed by diagonal walks, the heart of U-M

the-earle.text: The Earle opened on December 13, 1977 as a jazz club serving light fare, then remade itself in 1979 into the candlelit French and Italian country restaurant it still is. Its wine list runs past 1,200 selections and has earned Wine Spectator recognition 35 years running; live jazz plays five nights a week, with solo performers midweek starting at 7 p.m.
the-earle.descriptor: French and Italian country cooking at 121 W. Washington, with live jazz five nights a week

the-garage-bar.text: Brothers Matt and Dennis Tice opened the Garage Bar in 2016 beside their Pizza House on Church Street, on the spot where the restaurant parks its delivery cars. Massive overhead doors roll open onto Church and a cyclone-fence back wall lets the breeze through; Matt Tice described the idea as "like a giant tailgate." It pours 32 beers on tap.
the-garage-bar.descriptor: Open-air bar at Pizza House on Church St. with 32 taps and roll-up doors

the-grotto-watering-hole.text: It opened in January 2015 as the Beer Grotto, a compact sister to the Dexter bar, at 303 S. Ashley on the corner of Ashley and Liberty. Thirty-six rotating taps lean heavily on Michigan breweries like Short's, Kuhnhenn and Greenbush, and you can fill a growler to take home — the draw is the tap list, the cozy loft and the patio.
the-grotto-watering-hole.descriptor: Craft beer bar at Ashley & Liberty with 36 rotating taps and a patio

the-hen.text: Chris Fronimos, a Chicago native, opened the downtown cafe in 2021 as The Stray Hen and later dropped the "stray." He has since spun off The Hen on the Fly at 1906 Packard, a carryout-first version he describes as being for the impatient — he dislikes watching other people's orders get built ahead of his.
the-hen.descriptor: Breakfast-and-lunch cafe in downtown Ann Arbor, open since 2021

the-jagged-fork.text: The Ann Arbor storefront is one of six Jagged Forks around southeast Michigan — the others in Grosse Pointe Farms, Rochester Hills, West Bloomfield, Lathrup Village and Dearborn Heights — all working the same comfort-food breakfast and lunch menu of pancakes, omelets and sandwiches.
the-jagged-fork.descriptor: Metro Detroit breakfast-and-lunch chain's Ann Arbor spot on S. Main St

the-jefferson-market.text: The little brick storefront across from Bach Elementary is a survivor from the pre-zoning era, when small markets dotted Ann Arbor's neighborhoods; since then it's been a party store, a cakery and a Mighty Good Coffee shop. Ed Green and Angie May, who met working at a small Berkeley diner, took it over in 2019 and reopened it after just three days closed.
the-jefferson-market.descriptor: All-day breakfast and brunch cafe at 609 W. Jefferson on the Old West Side

the-last-word.text: The entrance is easy to walk past: a dark red door recessed off West Huron like a speakeasy's. Inside there are no TV screens, just a bookshelf, walls of vintage art in frames and live music on Thursday nights. The room has had several lives before this one, first as the Oyster Bar & Spaghetti Machine, then as Goodnight Gracie.
the-last-word.descriptor: Cocktail and whiskey bar behind a speakeasy-style red door on W. Huron

the-lunch-room-bakery-cafe.text: The Lunch Room began as dinner parties and pop-ups in 2010, became a cart at Mark's Carts downtown in 2011, and opened a Kerrytown restaurant in August 2013. This all-vegan bakery and cafe followed in February 2015, on the ground floor of the Huron Towers apartments a few steps from the Huron River, U-M North Campus and the VA hospital.
the-lunch-room-bakery-cafe.descriptor: All-vegan bakery and cafe in Huron Towers, near U-M North Campus

the-ponds-park.text: The city acquired the original 1.66 acres in 1989 when the Georgetown apartments were developed, then expanded the park in 1999 with two lots from the Hearthstone Subdivision, bringing it to about 2.25 acres. The northern half is left natural — trails under tall cottonwoods — while the south end has a playground with an accessible swing and a flower garden kept up by a park adopter group.
the-ponds-park.descriptor: Playground, garden and cottonwood trails off Emerald Ave near Packard

the-ravens-club.text: The Main Street building dates to 1868 and has housed a drinking establishment ever since. The current Ravens Club took over in 2011 and built out its Whiskey Library — bourbon, rye, Scotch, Irish and Japanese — plus live jazz on Sunday evenings with no cover.
the-ravens-club.descriptor: Craft cocktail and whiskey bar at 207 S. Main in an 1868 building

the-wave-field.text: Maya Lin's first experiment with earthworks, completed in 1995 outside the FXB Aerospace Engineering Building on North Campus. She sculpted the lawn into rows of grass swells after studying diagrams of fluids in motion and photographs of ocean waves — an attempt to capture and freeze the motion of water in earth rather than on film. She built a larger, four-acre version at Storm King Art Center in 2008.
the-wave-field.descriptor: Maya Lin earthwork of rolling grass waves on U-M's North Campus

the-west-end-grill.text: Zagat ranked the West End Grill fifth among metro Detroit restaurants, calling it a modern American spot in Ann Arbor; every place in that top ten scored between 28 and 29 out of 30. It still serves dinner nightly at 120 W. Liberty.
the-west-end-grill.descriptor: Modern American fine dining at 120 W. Liberty downtown

thurston-nature-center.text: Founded in 1964 on the recommendation of U-M professor Bill Stapp — widely called the founder of environmental education — the center wraps 24 acres of trails, oak savannah, prairie and rain gardens around a seven-acre pond. Two islands built from dredged pond sediment in 2015 give birds a place to land, and snapping turtles, herons, egrets and merganser ducks turn up in summer.
thurston-nature-center.descriptor: 24-acre nature preserve and seven-acre pond in the Thurston neighborhood

tienda-la-libertad.text: A no-frills Latin American grocery at 2231 W. Liberty stocked with products from Mexico, Brazil, Argentina and beyond, with a food counter sharing the space where you order tacos, burritos, enchiladas and meat dishes to eat in or take away.
tienda-la-libertad.descriptor: Latin American market with a taco counter on W. Liberty St

tios-mexican-cafe.text: Tios served Mexican food downtown from 1986, working with local farmers and vendors, until it closed after 40 years at 401 E. Liberty. In the notice on its own site the team pointed regulars still after the #4 and the house dressing to social media, hinting the food may resurface at farmers markets and other venues.
tios-mexican-cafe.descriptor: Mexican cafe at 401 E. Liberty St. from 1986; closed after 40 years

tk-wu.text: A family-run downtown Chinese kitchen on East Liberty whose menu leans on roasted Beijing duck, salt-and-pepper pork chops, garlic shrimp and jalapeño chicken.
tk-wu.descriptor: Family-run Chinese restaurant on E. Liberty St downtown

tmaz-taqueria-dexter.text: Cesar Hervert and Ana Trinidad opened the first Tmaz in 2011 in a two-table space on Packard; the name honors Trinidad's hometown of Temascalcingo, Mexico, known locally as Tmaz. This second shop opened in early 2021 in the former Aamani's Smokehouse space — despite the name, it's on Dexter Ave. in Ann Arbor, not in Dexter — and came with a fryer, which added flautas and chilaquiles to the menu.
tmaz-taqueria-dexter.descriptor: Mexican taqueria on Dexter Ave., the second Tmaz location

tomukun-korean-bbq-noodle-bar.text: Two sibling restaurants share one address on E. Liberty: Tomukun Korean BBQ, with table-top grills, classic Korean soul food and Asian draft beer, soju and makgulli, and Tomukun Noodle Bar, serving ramen, pho, udon, stir-fry and pork buns alongside Asian beers, sake and soju.
tomukun-korean-bbq-noodle-bar.descriptor: Korean BBQ with tabletop grills plus a noodle bar at 505 E. Liberty

totoro-sushi.descriptor: Sushi, tempura and teriyaki on S. State St. downtown

tuebingen-parkway.text: Named for Tübingen, Germany, which became Ann Arbor's first sister city in 1965 through Eisenhower's People to People program — both are college towns sitting next to bigger industrial cities. The seven acres are mostly natural area with unpaved trails and exercise stations, but the draw is one of the city's only two bike parks: a dirt pump track plus several downhill dirt jump lines.
tuebingen-parkway.descriptor: 7-acre natural area with a dirt bike pump track, northeast side

twigs.descriptor: U-M residential dining hall hidden inside Oxford Housing on Oxford Road

two-songs-bakery-cafe.text: Jenny Song and her mother Youn ran Songbird Cafe for 11 years before selling it, and kept baking wholesale out of its kitchen; in October 2024 they came back with a storefront of their own on S. Industrial. It's a counter with seating for about a dozen, stocked with gluten-free and vegan pastries and desserts plus shelves of Korean packaged snacks and groceries.
two-songs-bakery-cafe.descriptor: Korean-influenced gluten-free and vegan bakery on S. Industrial Hwy

umma-cafe.text: UMMA opened the cafe in early June 2019 as a two-year pilot with Michigan Dining, made possible by longtime museum volunteer and advocate Paola Luptak and aimed at drawing students and Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti community members into the building. The counter serves espresso drinks, tea and signature UMMA coffee alongside salads, sandwiches, pastries and bento boxes, with events, talks and concerts planned in the space.
umma-cafe.descriptor: Museum cafe at UMMA, 525 S. State St., run with Michigan Dining

union-rec.text: Union Rec opened November 30, 2022 inside the millwork shop of Fingerle Lumber, the S. Main Street lumberyard that ran 88 years before closing in 2019. Owners Ann Stevenson and Curt Catallo built the room around the idea of "the best sleepover" — salvaged, mismatched reupholstered chairs in clashing prints ringing a fireplace in the middle of the floor.
union-rec.descriptor: Comfort food and cocktails in the old Fingerle Lumber shop on S. Main

unitea.text: UniTea opened in July 2021 in the Maynard House storefront Iorio Gelato had long occupied, launched by owner Ethan Pham and his cousin Terry Phung, who already ran the Vietnamese restaurant VKitchen. The "uni" stands for university — Pham wanted a spot near campus instead of another strip mall. Strong Vietnamese iced coffee anchors the menu.
unitea.descriptor: Bubble tea and Vietnamese iced coffee cafe at 522 E. William since 2021

university-of-michigan-golf-course.text: Perry Maxwell drew the original plans and Alister MacKenzie reworked them, adding some 350 yards, the quirky par-five 3rd and the horseshoe-shaped 6th green. The course opened in 1931, hosted the 1947 NCAA golf championship, and got a $3.3 million restoration in 1992.
university-of-michigan-golf-course.descriptor: MacKenzie/Maxwell 1931 campus course, home of the Wolverine golf teams

university-of-michigan-museum-of-art.text: One of the largest university art museums in the U.S., UMMA holds more than 20,000 works — Picasso, Monet, Whistler, Kara Walker — inside Alumni Memorial Hall, a building dedicated in 1910 as a Civil War memorial. A 2009 wing by architect Brad Cloepfil more than doubled the museum's size, and admission is free.
university-of-michigan-museum-of-art.descriptor: Free university art museum in 1910's Alumni Memorial Hall on S. State St.

writtenFor.name: University of Michigan Museum of Art

university-of-michigan-museum-of-natural.text: The university's natural history collections date to 1837 and have been on public display since 1881. The museum spent nearly 90 years in Albert Kahn's Ruthven Museums Building before reopening in 2019 in the new Biological Sciences Building, with over 45,000 square feet of exhibits and its signature mastodons — including a mastodon trackway, the largest on display in the world. Admission is free.
university-of-michigan-museum-of-natural.descriptor: Free natural history museum in the Biological Sciences Building on Central Campus

writtenFor.name: University of Michigan Museum of Natural History

uplift.text: Uplift opened in 2024 at 210 S. First, in the ground-floor space that had been the Millennium Club, as a full-time queer neighborhood bar rather than a once-a-month night. Co-owner Saharsh Hajela's pitch: a place where you can be unapologetically yourself. The week runs trivia, karaoke, dance parties and Sunday drag brunch, with the food coming from CIRC upstairs.
uplift.descriptor: LGBTQ+ bar on S. First St. with drag nights, karaoke and Sunday drag brunch

upstairs-at-crazy-wisdom.text: Crazy Wisdom has been Ann Arbor's bookstore of consciousness and alternative spirituality since 1982, owned from 1989 by Bill Zirinsky and Ruth Schekter until it closed in February 2022 after 40 years. A new Crazy Wisdom has since opened at 114 S. Main, where the upstairs that was long the tea room now runs as an art gallery and event space for readings, workshops and ceremonies.
upstairs-at-crazy-wisdom.descriptor: Upstairs gallery and event space above the Crazy Wisdom bookstore, 114 S. Main

venue-by-4m.text: An unusual hybrid on S. Industrial: 4M Consolidated Brands runs one space that works as coworking desks, private offices and meeting rooms by day, and an event venue, bar and international cafe by night — with live music Friday and Saturday and a Sunday jazz brunch.
venue-by-4m.descriptor: Coworking space, bar and cafe with live music on S. Industrial Hwy

vertex-coffee-roasters.text: Vertex opened on S. University in June 2019 and roasts all of its beans at its own roastery in Milan, Michigan, adding a second cafe in Ypsilanti in early 2024. The queer- and woman-owned shop builds its identity around quality, sustainability and community — zero-waste practices and public events as much as espresso.
vertex-coffee-roasters.descriptor: Queer- and woman-owned coffee bar at 1335 S. University since 2019

vinology.text: Kristin Jonna and her father John — the family behind Merchant of Vino — opened Vinology in 2006, as part of the redevelopment that brought the Mayer Schairer Building on Main Street back to life with two added stories on top.
vinology.descriptor: Wine bar and restaurant at 110 S. Main in the historic Mayer Schairer Building

virginia-park.descriptor: Five-acre neighborhood ballfield park lined with tall sycamores, west of downtown

waterworks-park.text: Allen Creek still runs underneath Waterworks Park — the stream was channeled underground in the 1920s, right about when the city acquired the land in 1927. The Western Kiwanis Club installed the first play equipment in 1978, and Ann Arbor Farm & Garden adopted the park in 2023 to tend its native-plant beds.
waterworks-park.descriptor: Shady 1.5-acre neighborhood park with a playground between 7th and 8th streets

wellington-park.text: A 1.19-acre neighborhood park on Ann Arbor's west side — abundant mature shade trees, an open grassy field with a baseball and softball field, a playground and a Little Free Library. The land was set aside for public use by the neighborhood's own developer, transferred to the Parks Department in 1948, and approved for development by City Council in 1951.
wellington-park.descriptor: 1.19-acre neighborhood park with a ball field off Bruce St, west side

west-park.text: Land here has been Ann Arbor parkland since 1908, assembled over a century in 28 separate acquisitions. The bandshell, a home-grown structure designed by the city's Department of Public Works in 1938, hosted concerts for decades until it was closed in 2021 over structural issues. The park also holds a 1925 pergola, two city champion trees, and a stretch of historic Native American trail.
west-park.descriptor: 27-acre park west of downtown with a 1938 bandshell

wheeler-park.text: It began as the Summit Street playground: before the turn of the century the site was a hitching station for horse-driving teamsters, and later neighbors used the leveled plot as an ice rink. After fifteen years of negotiation the city bought the adjoining salvage yard in 1975, and the expanded park opened in 1977; in 1987 it was renamed for Albert Wheeler, Ann Arbor's first Black mayor, a U-M professor and civil rights leader who had championed it.
wheeler-park.descriptor: Just-under-two-acre Kerrytown park with a playground and basketball court

winewood-thaler-park.text: The city bought the land in 1974 and development began in 1977. The 1.72-acre park squeezes in two playground areas, a merry-go-round, a half-court, a woodchip nature trail, and a native wildflower and edible-landscaping garden, plus a paved path connecting Winewood to Carolina Avenue that the city clears in winter.
winewood-thaler-park.descriptor: West-side pocket park between Winewood and Thaler Aves, with two playgrounds

woodbury-park.text: From 1916 to 1961 this land was the University of Michigan's Botanical Gardens. After the gardens relocated, the Woodbury Gardens apartment development began in 1969, and the nearby streets were named to honor the site's botanical heritage.
woodbury-park.descriptor: 2.5-acre park with tennis courts on Astor Ave, south of Stadium Blvd

wsg-gallery.text: The initials stand for Washington St. Gallery, where the artists' collective opened in 1999 — but WSG has been nomadic ever since, moving to Liberty St. in 2003 and S. Main St. in 2008 before the pandemic closed it in 2020. It reopened in June 2021 on E. Ann St., in a nineteenth-century brick storefront in what was the heart of Ann Arbor's Black business district and once housed Clint's Club. Fourteen members show painting, ceramics, fiber, jewelry, photography and prints.
wsg-gallery.descriptor: Artist-owned downtown gallery, a 14-member collective since 1999

wurster-park.text: The land was a gravel pit at the end of Fourth St. before the city named it in 1955 for Ernst M. Wurster, an Ann Arbor mayor from 1917 to 1919. Two champion trees stand here: a black oak on the north end thought to be 200-300 years old, and a chinkapin oak that is the largest of its species in Michigan. There's also a sand volleyball court, playground and horseshoe pit.
wurster-park.descriptor: 5.5-acre Old West Side park with sand volleyball and champion oaks

yogurt-rush.text: It's a store within a store. In 2009 Amer's Delicatessen owner Amer Bathish invented the yogurtrush brand and gave over part of his State St. and Church St. shops to expanded self-serve dairy bars, offering sour and non-sour flavors sold by the ounce at 49 cents — deliberately under Swirlberry's 65 cents down the block. It made Amer's the fourth frozen-dairy player on the State Street campus strip.
yogurt-rush.descriptor: Self-serve frozen yogurt bar inside Amer's Delicatessen, 312 S. State

york-food-drink.text: YORK occupies the Packard St. building that was once the Big Ten Party Store and then Morgan & York, the wine-and-deli shop Tommy York co-owned with Matt Morgan; he now runs his own place in the same space. It pours estate-bottled wines, bottled beer and espresso, builds cheese and charcuterie boards and European-inspired sandwiches, and hosts Ricewood's Texas-style barbecue out of its kitchen.
york-food-drink.descriptor: Wine, cheese and charcuterie bar on Packard St, with a BBQ pop-up kitchen

yost-ice-arena.text: Built in 1923 as the Fielding H. Yost Field House and converted to an ice rink in 1973, Yost seats about 5,800 and is nicknamed "the Cathedral of College Hockey." Michigan's basketball team played here before Crisler opened in 1967.
yost-ice-arena.descriptor: 1923 field house turned college hockey barn, home of Michigan hockey

zingermans-deli.text: Paul Saginaw and Ari Weinzweig opened Zingerman's in 1982 serving traditional Ashkenazi deli sandwiches; the numbered menu's #18 Georgia Reuben, a grilled turkey Reuben with coleslaw and housemade Russian dressing, is the deli's second-biggest seller. It grew into the Zingerman's Community of Businesses — nine Ann Arbor companies, about 500 employees and $40 million a year as of 2012. It was nearly called Greenberg's until another business objected.
zingermans-deli.descriptor: Ann Arbor deli serving traditional Ashkenazi Jewish food since 1982

zingermans-next-door-cafe.text: The cafe half of Zingerman's Delicatessen, the Detroit Street deli Paul Saginaw and Ari Weinzweig founded in 1982 and grew into a whole family of Ann Arbor food businesses.
zingermans-next-door-cafe.descriptor: Cafe alongside Zingerman's Delicatessen on Detroit Street in Ann Arbor

zingermans-roadhouse.text: Zingerman's opened the Roadhouse in 2003 as part of its Community of Businesses, serving regional American food: pit barbecue, fried chicken and mac and cheese. It won a James Beard Award for Best Chef: Great Lakes in 2011 and was a James Beard finalist again in 2019 for Outstanding Service and 2020 for Outstanding Hospitality.
zingermans-roadhouse.descriptor: Regional American roadhouse on Jackson Ave — barbecue, fried chicken, mac and cheese
